projectOutComesReport:
In this project, we introduced new system topologies, control techniques, passive designs, and integrated circuits to achieve faster response, higher density, and higher efficiency in switching voltage regulators. Multiple chips were designed and fabricated to obtain silicon measurement results. Specifically: 

1) A multi-phase integrated voltage regulator supporting more than 3 A of current and achieving 93.9% peak efficiency is proposed. With the new current-mode Double-Adaptive-Bound (DAB) control and burst-mode operation addressing small-signal bandwidth limitations, the converter exhibited less than 100 mV voltage droop under 2.85 A/ns load transients. The introduced real-time adaptive phase-count control also helped optimize the power efficiency in a wide loading range.

2) An integrated single-inductor multiple-output (SIMO) voltage regulator is proposed to reduce the number of power inductors for cost and form-factor reduction, while providing more regulated output rails. To enhance dynamic speed, a “Buffet-Like” nonlinear control is introduced to overcome small-signal limitations, and a digital LDO per output provides an alternative current path to address large-signal limitations, achieving more than 7X improvement in load-transient handling capability compared with state-of-the-art designs at the time. Efficiency optimization techniques are also proposed, resulting in a measured 96.1% peak efficiency with a miniature power inductor.

3) A 3-level single-inductor multiple-output voltage regulator is proposed with on-chip implementation of passive components, including the power inductor and flying capacitor, to reduce parasitic inductance and resistance for improved reliability, faster response, and higher power efficiency. A new design methodology of nonlinear control for hybrid capacitive and inductive switchings converters, namely the “state-based” control, is proposed to eliminate the small-signal bandwidth limitations of traditional linear control methodologies, thereby enhancing dynamic response. The converter was verified with 1A/1.5 ns load transients in measurement, showing less than 50 mV droops. The load-transient handling capability exceeded that of the state-of-the-art at the time by more than 4X.

4) We also conducted analysis and comparison of different types of hybrid capacitive and inductive switching voltage regulators for achieving higher voltage conversion ratios, and proposed a new universal steady-state and small-signal analysis methodology applicable to any non-resonant hybrid switching voltage regulators, ensuring stability while optimizing dynamic performance.

The results have been disseminated to the community through conference and journal publications, as well as invited talks in industry. Moreover, this work trained multiple graduate and undergraduate students. Hands-on workshops were also delivered to K–12 students in collaboration with Science Bound. Lastly, this project also contributed to improvements in both undergraduate and graduate curricula by incorporating new course materials and research findings into classroom teaching.

abstractText:
With a goal to form a community of Smart and Connected Farms (SCFs), this innovative project aims to establish a Smart Integrated Farm Network for Rural Agricultural Communities (SIRAC). The goal is to improve timely data sharing and knowledge exchange among farmers community for coordinated responses to production threats (weed, disease, insect, pest, weather), ensuring profitability. The project will develop a flexible, scalable and efficient communication infrastructure for SCFs; provide privacy-preserving data analytics across farms for community-level decision-making; establish community of practice to facilitate learning and feedback among farmers/scientists, trusted data and technology acceptance; and demonstrate economic benefit to SCFs.

The novelty of SIRAC project lies in the holistic integration of multiband dynamic spectrum access (DSA) technology for rural connectivity and community decision-making, with social translational research to address adoptability, trust, and risk preferences, and economics research to benefit farmers. Mobile crowd sensing will improve trustworthiness and decision accuracy of information spread. Fundamental contributions involve the development of novel routing algorithms, privacy-preserving machine learning techniques, and affordable communication infrastructure with unlicensed multiple spectrum bands to create SCF community for efficient data sharing. Translational research model with behavioral experiments will identify social and economic incentives for farmers/stakeholders leading to technological innovations.

The SIRAC framework has the potential to provide tremendous impacts, as it can be adapted and replicated in different rural areas. The proposed (rural) communications technology will apply to a broad range of smart and connected communities. The assessment of social and economic incentives for farmers and other stakeholders will facilitate participation in SCF network. The project will motivate next generation of scientists and farmers to contribute to smart agricultural communities with innovative solutions. Results will be disseminated via web lecture series, invited talks, a dedicated project website, participants and other communities, extension field days, conferences and workshops, and peer-reviewed journals.

The SIRAC repository will maintain computational codes, models, real world and simulation data, experimental results for two years after the project period is over. The project website will provide two levels of access: Public and Login Required. An account can be created via registration with no charge. Additionally, developed codes and simulation models will be available to the community through the Iowa State University’s digital repository. Permission will be granted to freely use and distribute the anonymized data from simulations and field experiments with due acknowledgement of the copyright notice and the authors.

projectOutComesReport:
The SIRAC project developed an innovative smart-farming network to enhance pest management and agricultural decision-making in rural communities. By combining cutting-edge technology with research from human sciences and economic analysis, this project developed practical solutions to help farmers tackle pest-related challenges in crop production. It provided guidelines for farmer-to-farmer collaboration mechanisms and economic considerations. The project also involved strong collaboration with various universities and the Iowa Soybean Association, representing the interests of thousands of farmers.

Key Technical Innovations and Outcomes

Smart Learning Framework: The project developed a new way to use machine learning for agriculture called a dynamic split learning framework. This system employs a Q-learning agent to smartly distribute work across different devices while keeping farm data safe. This method significantly reduced energy consumption by up to 86% compared to older approaches, while ensuring that sensitive information remained private. The system was tested on insect classification using advanced neural network architectures and achieved a high accuracy of 94% with the MobileNetV2 model.

Drone Technology: The project optimized drone-based data collection using advanced algorithms to efficiently plan flight paths, solving the Traveling Salesman Problem. This resulted in a 17% increase in accuracy and reduced energy use for drone operations compared to traditional methods. A testbed was created with 29 solar UV sensors attached to Raspberry Pi devices, allowing for effective testing of data collection strategies in agriculture.

Pest Density Forecasting: A multimodal deep learning system was designed to predict populations of soybean aphids by combining weather, vegetation, and soil data. This system achieved an R² score of 0.77, showing it works much better than simpler models. An analysis confirmed that each type of data added valuable insights for accurate predictions. Building on this analysis, a multi-agent crop assistant was developed, which could determine whether applying pesticides would be beneficial, achieving an impressive 96% accuracy in its recommendations.

Disease Detection Infrastructure: The project improved communication systems for detecting crop diseases by using LoRaWAN technology. The iCrop framework can classify diseases with high accuracy while being affordable. A testbed using Raspberry Pi devices, RGB cameras, and LoRa communication helped to effectively monitor crop health.

Human Sciences and Community Engagement

A vital aspect of the SIRAC project is its collaboration with the Iowa Soybean Association, which ensured meaningful engagement with farmers. Focus groups and studies revealed important insights into farmers' preferences concerning smart farming technologies. Key findings include:

Trust Issues: Farmers typically prefer non-profit organizations, like universities and commodity boards, to manage their data instead of private companies, reflecting concerns over data privacy and control. Farmers emphasized the importance of good technical support, quick responses, clear communication, accessibility from providers, as well as adoption will succeed if they can see other farmers successfully use the tool/technology.

Valued Technology: The most appreciated benefit among farmers was effective field scouting, while peer-to-peer data sharing was less prioritized.

These findings highlight that issues of trust, transparency, and practical use are essential for farmers when adopting new digital agricultural technologies.

Economic Analysis and Network Design

Economic analysis showed varied benefits for farmers participating in the network. Gains per acre ranged from about $68 to $347 (simulated per-acre gain), based on different factors such as risk profiles and scouting precision. During extreme weather, with increased growing degree days, median benefits could rise to approximately $87 per acre, reflecting about 37% of average production costs. Additionally, analyzing network design demonstrated that selecting signals based on proximity significantly improved effectiveness, reducing average signal distance by over 90% and increasing potential gains to $518 per acre for those at the highest tiers. Farms with a higher infestation risk, less precise standalone scouting, and closer access to high-quality peers tend to capture the largest gains. This is useful for targeting participation and pricing strategies.

Innovation and Entrepreneurship

An essential outcome of the SIRAC project's innovation efforts was the development of a minimum viable product for automated insect detection, driven by insights from customer feedback through the I-Corps program. This solar-powered system includes: Cellular communication modules, Edge computing devices (Raspberry Pi), GPS sensors, 5MP camera that captures images from yellow sticky traps every four hours. The system is designed to operate continuously for nearly 40 hours on a single battery charge. Field testing in Iowa showcased its practical applications, with stakeholders including growers, entomologists, and agronomists expressing interest. Collaborative efforts are also in place with industry leaders like Microsoft for advancements in automated pest management systems and Bayer Crop Science for identifying insect-borne diseases.

SIRAC project focused on farmer community building around smart agriculture, integrating advanced technology and community engagement to provide farmers with vital tools for enhancing pest management, fostering economic benefits, and promoting innovative practices in farming.

abstractText:
This project will investigate the reliability and validity of forensic decision making in the context of the technique of fired cartridge case comparison. It does so by examining whether inconclusive forensic decisions result from truly ambiguous physical evidence or from non-evidentiary factors. The project additionally will study whether pattern evidence produced by two different sources is sufficiently distinct to be consistently detected by forensic examiners. 

The project will employ an experimental approach to test the validity of forensic analyses of fired cartridge cases. Through interrater reliability, the research will assess the tendency for multiple forensic examiners to reach similar conclusions when evaluating the same evidence. The project also will ascertain whether the toolmarks left on fired cartridge cases by two discrete weapons are sufficiently distinct to be detected by different examiners. These comparisons will enable the project to test the validity of pattern matching forensic techniques that necessarily rely on subjective human judgments. As this research addresses issues relevant to a multitude of forensic techniques, it will significantly advance knowledge about the probative value of decision making throughout the forensic sciences.

abstractText:
Suspensions of solid particles immersed in a fluid – either gas or liquid – are important in many industrial systems and in many natural processes.  Multiphase computational fluid dynamics to predict the behavior of these systems relies on making approximations to the appropriate equations.  As a result, some important phenomena, such as the aggregation of solid particles in the flow, are not accurately predicted.  The formation of particle clusters in gas-solid flows results from complex interactions of the particles with the gas and the particles with each other.  This collaborative Computational and Data-Enabled Science and Engineering (CDS&E) project will develop a modeling framework for particle clustering in gas-flow problems enabled by massive simulations using highly scalable codes.  Numerical techniques developed by the researchers at the three participating institutions will be integrated to formulate a consistent and scalable framework for solving problems in which particle clustering is significant.  The results will enable researchers to tackle problems involving particle clusters such as chemical looping combustion, biomass fast pyrolysis and carbon dioxide capture applications.  Computational data generated in the project will be available to researchers through a web-based interface.  The researchers will use the project to develop educational tools to engage a broad public audience, especially middle and high school students, in displays of the fundamental principles underlying flows of particle suspensions in a gas.

Particle-resolved Direct Numerical Simulation (PR-DNS), which can resolve microscale particle-fluid interactions and point-particle direct numeric simulation (PP-DNS), which can model inter-particle collisions, will be integrated with pseudo-spectral techniques, which have the potential to accelerate computations for gas-solid flows.  Highly scalable PR–DNS and PP-DNS codes will be developed to leverage new algorithmic advances in (a) turbulence simulation using the pseudo-spectral approach on heterogeneous architectures and (b) efficient scaling with number of particles in Eulerian-Lagrangian multiphase flow solvers to perform massive PR–DNS and PP-DNS of canonical clustering flows on scales needed to demonstrate particle clustering.  Consistent scalable closures will be developed for volume-filtered Eulerian-Lagrangian formulations and PP-DNS and PR-DNS.   A consistent averaging operation will be applied on the PR–DNS data that explicitly takes the resolved scales into account, resulting in new unclosed terms that have yet to be quantified in a two-phase context. Novel closure techniques using machine learning will be employed to evaluate the functional form of the new terms.  To maximize their impact on model development, the source codes and canonical multiphase flow data generated in this project will be archived in an open-access database available to the broader scientific community.

projectOutComesReport:
The development of affordable clean energy solutions is critical to meet limits on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions that drive anthropogenic climate change. Clean and affordable energy generation from biomass through technologies such as pyrolysis or chemical looping combustion involve the flow of gas with particles. This often results in particles forming clusters as they interact with the turbulent motion of the gas phase. This project is focused on advancing the understanding and prediction of turbulence-induced clustering of particles in particle-laden flows,

Computer models of particles interacting with a turbulent gas can be used to predict particle clustering provided they capture all the relevant physical and chemical interactions between particles and turbulent gas flow. These fully accurate models are called particle-resolved direct numerical simulation (PR-DNS) models. Even if we restrict our attention to just the physical interactions, these occur on scales that range from the size of a particle to the scale of the industrial device that can contain trillions of particles. Therefore, computers need to represent very small scale motions and also very large scale motions. The challenge is that accurately representing this wide range of scales of motion requires computers that can store very large amounts of data, and perform calculations extremely rapidly, so that we can get predictions in a timely manner. Even with today’s fastest supercomputers, such calculations can take months to years.

Therefore, there is interest in developing an approximate (but still highly accurate) representation of the gas phase using the volume-filtered Euler Lagrange (VFEL) model, which can perform these calculations on less specialized computers with rapid turnaround time on the order of days to a week. The focus of this project is on developing such approximate VFEL models that are consistent with the most accurate PR-DNS computer models, and which minimally increase computing burden as we increase the size of the problem we wish to solve.

However, in order to make the approximate VFEL model consistent with the fully accurate PR-DNS model, we need to establish the mathematical conditions under which the approximate VFEL is still a highly accurate representation. The project demonstrated that by requiring the consistency of a particular common variable: namely, the variance of the filtered particle volume fraction, we can effectively characterize particle clustering even in VFEL.

In order to demonstrate the validity of this approach, we needed to resort to a third model where an approximate (but still highly accurate) representation of the particle phase using the point particle direct numerical simulation (PP-DNS) model, which can perform calculations of particle clustering on leadership-class computers with rapid turnaround time on the order of days to a week.

This project utilized state-of-the-art computational tools, including the most accurate particle-resolved (PR) and the approximate point-particle (PP) direct numerical simulation data to investigate clustering mechanisms of inertial particles in turbulent particle-laden flows.

We found from analyzing the PP-DNS data on particle clustering that the history of particle interactions with the turbulent gas contribute to the formation of particle clusters. Inspired by this analysis, a scale-dependent path-history particle dynamics model that more comprehensively captures the clustering dynamics of inertial particles was proposed. This model accounts for both local and non-local contributions of the flow field and integrates the Kinematic Simulation-based Sub-Grid Model (KSSGM), which effectively predicts particle clustering for high-inertia particles. Through this model, we aim to bridge the gap between particle-scale and device-scale interactions of fluid and particles, ultimately improving the predictive capabilities of approximate VFEL models for simulating large-scale industrial systems.

These improved models will enable highly accurate simulation of particle clustering in gas-particle suspensions that constitute critical processes in different energy technologies and environmental flows. Such improved models will result in performance gains, improved efficiency, and reliability of industrial clean energy technologies. They will also enable better prediction of pollution arising from environmental disasters and impacts on air and water quality resulting from the effects of climate change.

abstractText:
Nontechnical Summary

This award is made on an EAGER proposal invited through the Quantum Algorithm Challenge Dear Colleague Letter. It supports research and education to develop and implement algorithms to run on quantum computers that currently exist or will exist in the near future. A perfect quantum computer is expected to solve certain problems of practical interest much faster than any conventional computer, also called a classical computer. Examples include factoring large numbers into primes with Shor's algorithm and using Lloyd's algorithm to predict the time evolution of an interacting quantum system away from equilibrium. The latter could help in optimization and design of new biomaterials, drugs, and functional quantum materials. While the past few years have brought tremendous progress in efforts to build a perfect quantum computer, the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) technology is potentially decades away from being able to run Shor's and Lloyd's algorithms at practically relevant scales. The underlying reason is that NISQ computers possess of the order of hundreds of qubits as opposed to the millions required to fully correct for errors that arise from noisy gate operations. This severely limits the complexity of quantum algorithms compatible with NISQ hardware and exposes a critical need for further algorithmic advancement to achieve practical quantum advantage.

In this project, the PIs develop algorithms tailored to NISQ quantum processing units (QPUs) that can address fundamental challenges in nonequilibrium physics. Specifically, the research team proposes new hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms to simulate nonequilibrium dynamics and highly excited states in novel materials such as disordered quantum magnets. The algorithms will be implemented on QPUs from IBM and Rigetti and carefully benchmarked against existing state-of-the-art quantum and classical algorithms. In addition to finding opportunities for near-term quantum advantage, this project will provide new insights into fundamental questions of how systems of interacting particles relax to thermal equilibrium and how they respond to strong external fields.

The educational component of this project addresses the national priorities of educating a quantum-enabled workforce and enhancing the participation and inclusion of traditionally underrepresented groups in STEM areas. Within this project, the PIs will educate and train one graduate student, one undergraduate student, and one postdoctoral scholar in applying quantum computing algorithms to challenging open scientific questions. The PIs will also design a hands-on outreach workshop on quantum computing and present it at "Go Further," a STEM career conference aimed at female middle- and high-school students. Finally, the PIs will create and maintain an online blog for the general public that highlights career options in quantum information science and informs readers about recent trends in quantum algorithms.



Technical Summary

This award is made on an EAGER proposal invited through the Quantum Algorithm Challenge Dear Colleague Letter. It supports research and education to develop and implement algorithms to run on quantum computers that currently exist or will exist in the near future. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computing devices have computing capabilities that are beyond the reach of any classical supercomputer, as has recently been demonstrated by the Google team. Whether they also offer a practical quantum advantage for calculations of interest in physics, chemistry or materials science is an open question. Simulations of nonequilibrium dynamics and highly excited states in quantum many-body systems are a promising yet challenging target, since classical algorithms for such simulations suffer from the exponential complexity and highly entangled nature of generic excited states. The development of resource-efficient quantum algorithms for current NISQ hardware can unlock their potential to address important challenges in nonequilibrium many-body physics.

Here, the PIs propose two novel variational quantum algorithms that are based on the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithm, which has been demonstrated on NISQ hardware. Instead of targeting ground states as in previous works, the PIs propose to use different cost functions to explore the manifold of highly excited and time-evolved quantum states. After careful benchmarking against known quantum and classical algorithms, both algorithms will be used to address fundamental open scientific questions in the fields of many-body localization, nonlinear response and nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly disordered and interacting quantum systems.

The project will advance the capabilities of variational algorithms beyond exploring properties of low-energy states. Results of this research will provide insights into the properties of highly excited states in strongly disordered interacting spin chains, and address the existence of many-body localized phases and mobility emulsions, which violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. The research team will also shed light on the correlation and entanglement properties of prethermal quantum states that emerge in post-quench dynamics and test the hypothesis that their temporal stability is related to a small energy variance, making them approximate eigenstates. Finally, by implementing efficient NISQ quantum algorithms for the computation of higher-order and out-of-time-ordered correlation functions, the PIs will determine whether these functions can disentangle effects of disorder and interactions on quasiparticle properties and explore the onset of quantum chaos in spin models. By addressing fundamental challenges in condensed matter physics, the research team will contribute to the open question of whether NISQ technology offers a practical quantum advantage.

projectOutComesReport:
This NSF EAGER award supported the development of new approaches to simulate complex problems in quantum physics by leveraging the power of quantum computers. Much of our knowledge of the quantum world is restricted to low-energy properties, for which a host of mathematical and computational approaches exist. Quantum computers provide one promising route to overcome the challenges of simulating phenomena beyond low energies, which includes understanding quantum matter at high temperatures or driven away from equilibrium. In this project, the principal investigators (PIs) focused on devising algorithms for quantum computers to simulate such phenomena.


The research undertaken during the award proceeded along two related directions. The first is to advance a class of algorithms, known as variational quantum algorithms, that rely on having a good "guess" for the form of the quantum state that the simulation is targeting. The PIs applied this idea to two problems. First, they formulated a variational approach to simulating high-temperature properties of quantum systems. This class of algorithms may provide promising new tools to perform such simulations on quantum hardware, and may even hint at new approaches that can be undertaken with classical computer simulations. Second, they used a combination of variational and direct simulation techniques for nonequilibrium dynamics. Specifically, the PIs proposed to leverage direct simulation on the quantum device to propagate the quantum system's state for a limited time (set by the "coherence time" of the quantum device, which describes the time over which quantum information within the quantum computer remains stable). Then, the evolved state is "compressed" down into a variational form defined by a tractable number of parameters. This variational approximation can then be reconstructed during a new run of the quantum device, effectively extending the reachable simulation time beyond the coherence time of the device. The PIs and their team demonstrated an implementation of this algorithm on current quantum computers.


The second approach considered within this award is to supplement direct simulation approaches with classical data postprocessing techniques that can help to reduce the effect of hardware noise on the final answer. These postprocessing techniques collectively go under the name of "quantum error mitigation" (QEM). Using a few particular quantum dynamics problems as test cases, the PIs and their team tested the efficacy of several general QEM techniques on present-day quantum hardware. Their key finding was that, given the error rates of present-day devices, general QEM approaches alone are not sufficient to extract the relevant physics from the simulations. However, supplementing general QEM methods with problem-tailored insights, which leverage physical knowledge of the specific problem and measurable quantities being simulated, can produce compelling results. With their quantum simulations, the PI and their team used these methods to push simulations of quantum dynamics to the edge of the current state of the art.


Finally, this EAGER award also contributed to quantum workforce development in several ways. First, it directly supported undergraduate, graduate, and postdoctoral researchers to work on problems at the forefront of quantum computing. It also gave these researchers the opportunity to hone their communication skills by writing papers and giving presentations at conferences. Second, the PIs designed a quantum outreach module around the game "Quantum TiqTaqToe," originally developed as a mobile app by quantum physicists at Caltech. Aimed at female-identifying middle- and high-school students, the module includes a brief presentation introducing quantum mechanics and proceeds to engage the students by having them play the game against each other and a team of facilitators recruited from a pool of interested undergraduate, graduate, and postdoctoral physicists. The PIs extensively tested the module at a semiannual science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) workshop run by Iowa State University's Program for Women in Science and Engineering. The workshop received positive feedback. The PIs look forward to refining this workshop and developing new ways to drive interest in STEM with outreach around quantum physics topics.

abstractText:
Each year, in the US, emergencies cast devastating impacts on the civil and technical infrastructure, resulting in loss of human life, social and economic disturbances, and environmental damage. Because incidents are all different, first responders improvise when plans do not readily address a situation, where plans refer to documents detailing rules, standard operating procedures, roles, and organizational structures or any agreed-upon courses of action. Despite the importance of improvisation to emergency response, there exists a lack of accumulated knowledge on emergency improvisation, thus at the practice level it becomes difficult to transfer improvisation knowledge and skills from veterans to novices who are in need of such knowledge. An inability to properly improvise creates risks of response operation delays, inefficient allocation of resources, insufficient protection of operational safety, and mismanagement of crisis information. This project will explore the role of information technology (IT) in enabling and supporting emergency response improvisation. It will also investigate how organizational attributes and task-environment factors moderate the effects of IT support on improvisation. Expected research findings will guide IT vendors to develop new tools that offer improved support on emergency improvisation; help the emergency response community create organizational strategies and practices that better leverage IT for improvisational purpose.

This project will adopt and extend Activity Theory, a framework that is often used to describe collective actions, to the emergency improvisation context – we term this Crisis Response AT (CRAT). We will center our study of improvisation on upper to mid range Emergency Operating Centers (EOC) where IT could play a role in supporting improvisation. To collect a rich account of emergency response improvisation, the PIs will conduct interviews and focus-group studies of emergency response managers. The PIs will analyze the collected qualitative data and uncover major issues of improvisation, which are expected to result in a better understanding of how IT can be best used to address individual issues of improvisation. Following the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, in addition, the proposal will explore important organizational and task environment factors that may moderate, either support or hinder, the effect of IT on emergency response improvisation. An online survey will be used to collect data from EOCs nationwide and test hypotheses derived from the qualitative work and theory. Survey data will be analyzed using advanced statistical methods. Finally, the PIs will develop and distribute a toolkit to help EOC managers develop and evaluate IT initiatives that support improvisation. This toolkit will be validated by emergency practitioners.

abstractText:
This project supports secondary mathematics teachers in teaching mathematical modeling practices to an Emergent Bilingual (EB) population. EB students in linguistically diverse mathematics classrooms are frequently limited to procedural, rote instruction, despite research-based recommendations that suggest that EBs' mathematical and linguistic proficiency can benefit from engaging in complex mathematical tasks based on real-life situations. The project will support teacher capacity for implementing mathematical modeling lessons by engaging teachers in co-planning and co-teaching with researchers skilled in EB mathematics instruction. The project will collect information about the quality of mathematics instruction in modeling lessons, what students learn, and how teachers changed in how they position EB students as knowers and doers of mathematics. The outcomes of this project will be a framework for teaching mathematical modeling to EB students, teacher professional development materials that can be used widely to support EB mathematics teachers, and a massive open online course (MOOC) for teachers to support their continued learning about teaching mathematics modeling to EB students.

The project draws on three important constructs related to teaching mathematics to emergent bilingual (EB) students: research on the mathematics education of EB students; research on mathematical modeling; and positioning theory. Related to mathematics education of EB students, the project supports teachers in enacting high-quality instruction that incldues high cognitive demand tasks, encourages EBs to engage in and explain their problem solving process, and complements that work with linguistic and contextual supports that support EB students' entry into the tasks. Related to mathematical modeling, the project makes use of the conceptualization of modeling as a vehicle for content (as compared to mathematics content of its own), and envisions the use of modeling practices as particularly supportive of EB students' learning of algebra.  In particular, the modeling-as-a-vehicle stance invites teachers to engage students in tasks that contain multiple mathematical representations, which has the potential to both build students' conceptual understandings of algebra and to strengthen EBs' language and communication skills in the context of mathematics. With respect to positioning theory, the project seeks to disrupt the finding that secondary mathematics teachers tend underestimate EB students' mathematical abilities due to their English proficiency standards, causing them to choose lower cognitive demand tasks for these students against established research-based recommendations. The project team will engage EB algebra and pre-algebra teachers in Des Moines Public schools in co-planning and co-teaching lessons using mathematical modeling practice.  This co-planning and co-teaching activity constitutes in-situ professional development for teachers.  Co-planning sessions, co-taught lessons, and regular teacher interviews will be recorded and analyzed for quality of instruction and changes in teacher positioning of EB students. The research team and teachers will co-analyze student learning data from observations and district-administered standardized assessments to better understand the impact of the modeling lessons on students' algebra learning and achievement. Eight teachers will participate in the work over the life of the project, each supporting EB classes of approximately 20 students per teacher. The outcomes of these analyses will guide the development fo a mathematical modeling framework for teaching EBs, teacher professional development materials made available for similar work in other schools and districts, and a massive open online course designed for teachers to develop their skills for teaching secondary mathematics to EB students.

abstractText:
Fast pyrolysis is a prominent technology in converting waste biomass to combustible gases and liquids; pyrolysis also occurs at the early stage of solid fuel combustion. Fast pyrolysis-derived liquid fuels are regarded as an economically feasible alternative to fossil fuels and some facilities for heat and power generation have been brought online in recent years. However, despite its promising potential, the development of fast pyrolysis has been hindered by the complexity of reactor conditions in biomass pyrolysis, and to date, methods capable of predicting the detailed processes are unavailable. The objectives of this project are to characterize accurately the behaviors of biomass particles and predict the product yields of a fast pyrolysis reactor by using high-fidelity numerical simulations. The proposed research activities will lead to advances in the fundamental science of biomass pyrolysis for energy applications. The educational activities are to engage K-12 science teachers in research in order to promote education on renewable energy. In the U.S., a significant number of K-12 science teachers have not majored in the physical sciences. The research training of K-12 science teachers can enrich their critical thinking and enable them to incorporate their new knowledge into their classroom teaching.

The proposed research plan is to conduct high-resolution simulations of biomass fast pyrolysis and to derive submodels for use in engineering CFD codes. A novel simulation approach, one that combines the lattice Boltzmann method, discrete element method, chemical kinetics, and particle shrinkage modeling, will be employed to describe the physicochemical evolution of biomass particles. Computational results will be validated by experimental data. Based on the simulation results, a drag coefficient model will be derived and tested. This work will address several scientific topics of paramount importance to biomass pyrolysis: physicochemical changes of particles, particle-particle and gas-particle interactions, and effects of particle properties and operating conditions on the pyrolysis products. The underlying difficulty of designing and optimizing an efficient biomass reactor is the lack of fundamental understanding of particle behaviors under realistic conditions. This research will characterize intra-particle transport, flow fields smaller than particle size, chemical reactions, and evolutions of particle size and properties. The resulting open-source code can be used by the scientific community as a baseline tool for further advanced numerical study on the pyrolysis of solid particles, e.g., coal, wood chips, municipal solid waste, or polymer materials.

abstractText:
Over one million international students study at US universities, and the majority study in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields. All need to communicate in English, which requires intelligible pronunciation. The conventional wisdom is that simple immersion in the English-speaking environment will, over time, improve pronunciation. Research, however, rejects this view: without instruction that is explicitly focused on pronunciation (e.g., the vowels in "bad" vs. "bed"), learners are only likely to improve within the first year in the new environment, and instruction is needed after that. Unfortunately, face-to-face pronunciation instruction is infrequent, thus making computer-assisted pronunciation training (CAPT) the best option for pronunciation training at scale. CAPT programs are common, but share a critical weakness of not providing effective feedback to the learner. This project will examine the usefulness of two complementary forms of pronunciation feedback in CAPT: explicit feedback (focused on delivering precise instruction to the learner about the location and nature of pronunciation errors) and implicit feedback (relying on the learner's ability to perceive their mispronunciations). 

To this end, the investigators will develop mispronunciation-detection algorithms that can highlight errors in the learner's speech (explicit feedback), and they will create accent-conversion algorithms that can generate personalized speech samples for the learner: their own voice producing native-speech (implicit feedback). Specifically, the investigators will develop a machine-learning framework to solve the problems of mispronunciation detection and accent conversion simultaneously.  Research in machine learning shown that solving multiple tasks simultaneously can improve learning efficiency and generalization performance, so long as the tasks are related. Thus, this award offers the potential to advance the state-of-the-art in both problems. The two forms of pronunciation feedback (explicit and implicit) will be integrated into a CAPT system that automatically adapts to the learner's current performance to maximize the benefits for the learner as they develop their accuracy. The system will use an adaptive tutoring algorithm to guide the learner in first establishing perception of their pronunciation difficulties and then enhancing their production accuracy.

projectOutComesReport:
NSF Outcomes Report for Award 2016984

This NSF-reported project was a collaborative effort between experts in computer science (a co-PI from Texas A&M), pronunciation teaching, and computer-assisted language teaching (two co-PIs from Iowa State). Building on our previous work on speech synthesis and pronunciation learning in Ding et al. (2019), the project examined feedback in computer-assisted pronunciation training (CAPT), exploring how different types of feedback affect language learner improvement in their pronunciation of vowel and consonant sounds. We planned to look at differences between implicit feedback (such as listening to an ideal model voice but without any further guidance) and explicit feedback (such as when pronunciation that deviates expected sounds is highlighted with instructional tips). We wanted to see how these types of feedback differed in the type of pronunciation improvement L2 learners achieve. Previous research suggested that effective feedback is an interaction of type of feedback and the goal of the instruction (e.g., specific corrections vs. raising a learner’s awareness of pronunciation errors).

 

To achieve our objectives, we developed two computer environments: first, we developed a back-end that could take audio data and correctly detect mispronounced vowel and consonant phonemes in foreign-accented speech; second, we had to develop an accessible CAPT environment where learners received both diagnosis and remediation of their pronunciation errors. The CAPT environment had to diagnose learners’ pronunciation errors and develop individualized training cycles providing different types of implicit and explicit feedback. The system was intended to adapt to each learner’s performance so practice could be autonomously followed without direct instructor involvement.

 

Our results were presented at a variety of international conferences in 2021 and beyond. In relation to the MPD algorithm, the project resulted in the development and refinement of the baseline MPD back-end, resulting in multiple publications. Later modifications to the MPD algorithm improved its speech synthesis capabilities such that speech synthesis could be performed with only a few sentences of speech data. (For comparison, Ding et al. 2019 required 100 sentences of spoken data for synthesis.) We tested the level of accuracy needed for the MPD system in a study in which listeners evaluated how accurate automatic computer-assisted pronunciation feedback had to be. Research has repeatedly shown that 100% accuracy is a nearly unreachable target. Our research (Silpachai et al., 2024) thus used a Wizard of Oz protocol in which a pronunciation expert provided “automated” feedback that was as close to 100% accurate as possible and provided within a few seconds, mimicking the feedback that could be provided by a computer. The expert feedback was either sent through to learners as intended (the 100% condition), changed randomly so that feedback was correct two of three times (the 66% condition), or changed to be accurate only one of three times (the 33% condition). The study showed that learners improved equally in the 100% and 66% conditions, but that the 33% condition did not result in improvements. In further studies, we examined whether the MPD algorithm could be used to identify errors in word stress (which are signaled by vowel mispronunciations) and to distinguish between the speech of children speaking English as a second language, children with speech pathology challenges, and children without either. Both of these studies showed that the MPD system needed additional modifications for children’s voices and for the identification of stress errors.

 

The project was impacted by two unforeseen events, the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and the release of generative AI applications in late 2022. Because we had initially planned to conduct in-person laboratory training sessions with language learners and to work together in teams within the same physical space, the impact of COVID-19 was immediate and challenging to navigate, leaving our teams playing catch-up as we designed new ways to approach system development and data collection. The second event was the surprising disruption caused by the release of advanced generative AI tools in November 2022. Although these applications are best known for their ability to generate text quickly, another feature relevant to our project involved speech synthesis capabilities, which can easily clone voices. Our speech synthesis work was intended to focus on vowel and consonant sounds, while generative AI tools excel at prosody in spoken language, but this distinction was not immediately clear in the publicity surrounding these developments.

References

Ding, S., Liberatore, C., Sonsaat, S., Rehman, I., Silpachai, A., Zhao, G., Chukharev- Hudilainen, E., Levis, J., & Gutierrez-Osuna, R. (2019). Golden Speaker Builder – An interactive tool for pronunciation training. Speech Communication, 115, 51-66.

abstractText:
New gene editing techniques promise significant benefits within the agricultural sector. However, realizing the full potential of these technologies will depend on how it is governed, and whether the public accepts it. Gene editing for agriculture and food poses public acceptance challenges due to its association with genetically modified organisms, scientific complexity, and social and ethical concerns. New governance forms for gene editing for agriculture and food will be necessary since existing regulatory instruments cannot deal with its complexity and novel risks, but it is unclear what those governance forms should be and if they would enhance public trust in the technology. To address these gaps, this project analyzes how key actors use competing collective visions of the future and the role of science within it to shape public trust and governance approaches for gene editing for agriculture and food. Findings will be broadly disseminated to key publics through a policy panel, digital storytelling projects, high school lesson plans, and in online publications. These innovative digital and online educational resources will advance public literacy and engagement with the scientific, social, and ethical issues surrounding gene editing for agriculture and food. Knowledge generated by this project will benefit a wide range of stakeholders, influencers, and publics who are engaged in governance efforts for gene editing for agriculture and food.

This is a comparative investigation of how the ways in which actors from key social groups imagine their technoscientific futures matter for the use and governance of gene editing technologies for agriculture and food. Multiple social science methods, including media content analysis, in-depth stakeholder interviews, deliberative workshops, and interpretive comparative methods, are used to investigate this emerging scientific controversy and develop ways to create more inclusive governance processes for decision making related to controversial and emergent technologies. Project goals include: (1) Identifying key visions for technoscientific futures and their proponents; 2) Assessing how key actors develop and use particular visions of the future to stabilize or disrupt public trust in gene editing technologies and their governance; 3) Comparing visions of the futures across cases; and 4) Engaging key actors in deliberative workshops to provide an assessment of findings and deliberate on inclusive governance approaches. Overall, the project will contribute to the theory and practice of Responsible Research and Innovation, and to scholarship in Science and Technology Studies on governance of emerging technologies.

projectOutComesReport:
Gene editing techniques, such as CRISPR/Cas9, have been heralded as powerful new tools that can accelerate innovations to deliver crops, livestock, and foods with a variety of novel and beneficial traits quickly, easily, and cheaply.  To gain public acceptance of gene editing in agriculture and food, proponents promote the technology by developing sociotechnical imaginaries related to gene editing in agriculture and food (GEAF). Imaginaries describe values and visions that proponents assert concerning what collective futures should emerge and the central role of sociotechnical systems, such as gene editing, in that future.  Proponents use sociotechnical imaginaries to frame gene editing as desirable, good, and in the public interest, counterposed against the risks of not using gene editing to realize these futures.  

Project goals were to identify and compare 1) key competing sociotechnical imaginaries within and between case study countries (US, Japan, Netherlands, Canada, New Zealand); 2) what social forces inform them; and 3) how they influence public acceptance and shape public and private efforts to govern GEAF, such as the development of laws, policies, international agreements, or food labels.

Our findings highlight the diverse social, cultural, and political considerations that inform efforts to promote gene editing and to address calls for more diverse input into the governance of gene editing in case study countries.  Through our content analysis of the media in the US, New Zealand, Canada, Netherlands and Japan, we found that news media in these countries reinforce a predominantly positive portrayal of the technology’s future, although variations in which imaginaries are most mobilized exist based on the regulatory status of gene editing and unique histories of civil society engagement around biotechnology in each country. By granting legitimacy to some narratives over others, the media supports gene editing as a desirable and necessary component of future agrifood systems, thereby limiting consideration of broader issues related to the technology’s development and application.

Through our qualitative content analysis of online communications documents published by civil society organizations in the US and EU who have publicly articulated opposition to some element of GEAF, we found key differences between the regions with regard to the types of participating actors, their diagnoses of relevant problems, and the degree and type of change that they promote related to food system reform. By explicitly rejecting biotechnologists’ characterization of gene editing as an accessible, democratizing tool with wide-ranging societal benefits, EU-based civil society organizations (CSO) are challenging the status quo of industrial agriculture and creating space for the consideration of social and ethical issues in its governance and application, which may enable more systemic reform. In contrast, US-based CSOs’ focus on individual consumers’ rights to make informed decisions about what they are purchasing does not necessarily question the role that biotechnology should play in agriculture more broadly, instead reflecting an acceptance that products of these techniques will eventually permeate through the food system. Differences in both coalitional and framing strategies reflect distinctive visions about the appropriate relationship between science, state, and society.  These differing strategies have significant implications for governance, public acceptance, and future development of agricultural gene editing in the US and the EU. 

We also explored how an educational lesson on agricultural biotechnology influences knowledge and attitudes toward different agricultural technologies among undergraduate students at two universities. Our story-based, systems-focused lesson was followed by a survey to assess impacts on knowledge and attitudes. We found that educational interventions can affect knowledge and attitudes surrounding agricultural biotechnology. Our study adds to the empirical evidence challenging the knowledge deficit model as we also found that more knowledge does not always lead to greater acceptance of a technology such as gene editing, as multiplenother factors shape acceptance and/or opposition.

We conducted deliberative workshops with key civil society actors to explore public engagement in gene editing governance across our case study countries.  We found that civil society actors believe that gene editing may offer solutions to food system and climate challenges, but it also brings risk of greater concentration of power in agricultural biotech companies, losses in seed and food sovereignty, and resulting fewer resources given to smaller farmers and agroecological farming systems. 

Our project findings expand the emerging field that bridges critical agrifood systems and STS scholarships by comparing GEAF sociotechnical imaginaries (and counter imaginaries) across several countries with distinctive regulatory contexts and political histories, and how and why these factors shape how some imaginaries become stabilized while others are marginalized or reconfigured.

abstractText:
Reusability of research data is central to successfully maximizing the benefits of public access to publicly funded research outputs.  The purpose of this EAGER proposal is to improve understanding of factors that lead to reusability of research data.  It proposes to do this by 1) developing a framework for understanding data reusability, 2) identify concomitant practices for improving data reusability, and 3) propose a path for accelerating the data reusability readiness of the research community.  The project would accomplish this through targeted research and feedback sought through a group meeting.  

Research teams at Iowa State University and the University of Virginia will pursue this goal by first gathering descriptive information on targeted research communities with different levels of maturity in their practices of research data sharing and reuse, as well as trusted repositories that have adopted practices for evaluating data sources prior to data ingest and reuse.  This descriptive information will inform a draft framework articulating common elements of data reuse, and processes for depositing data in ways that promote reusability.  The framework will also examine incentives and barriers to data reusability.  Feedback from a community meeting will inform subsequent refinement of the framework, which will be used in small scale tests using publicly accessible data sets and research groups at ISU and UVA.  The final version of the framework would include a discussion of strategies for accelerating the sharing of research data and the corresponding culture changes needed for success.

projectOutComesReport:
Fostering Impact and Ease in Producing and Reusing Publicly Accessible Research Data 

SM Nusser (Iowa State University), AM Mikytuck (Randolph-Macon College), G Korkmaz (Westat)

Our project sought to improve the reusability and impact of publicly accessible research data by 1) identifying context needed by researchers who use publicly accessible research data (data users) to be successful in understanding, evaluating and appropriately analyzing shared data sources; 2) outlining practices that help those who generate shared data (data producers) improve the quality of their data, reduce their effort in preparing data, and minimize reputational risks; and 3) developing a field-independent model of research practices in the data sharing and reuse cycle that fosters the success of all researchers.

Data users leverage an unexpectedly wide range of resources in assessing and using shared data. In addition to the widely cited need for metadata describing a data source’s contents, users rely on detailed information on study design, data generation methods, and code used to process and analyze the data source. They use this information to evaluate the credibility of the data source and to understand, evaluate and properly analyze the data source. Descriptions of data provenance and terms of use are key to outlining appropriate uses for the data source and any obligations that data user has in stewarding the shared data. Globally unique and persistent identifiers for the researcher, their institution and funders are used to assess the reputation of data producers and repositories where data are made public accessible. 

Data producers generally have limited understanding of context needed by data users and may not know how to reduce burden and minimize risks in preparing and quality data sources. Our work highlights the need to dedicate far more effort in planning for data sharing before the study begins to both reduce producer burden and foster data reusability. Planning for data sharing (as opposed to study design) involves specifying what digital objects will be shared with the data (e.g., study design, software code, data use agreement), how that information will be generated and updated throughout the research project, and how research outputs will be packaged and shared for reuse. Detailed planning not only enhances quality of the data and documentation, it provides the foundation for another key strategy – standardizing protocols and formats where possible and automating research processes to reduce burden and improve consistency throughout the research pipeline. Establishing workflows and tools for automation and standardization enables a third strategy: the internal sharing of digital objects among research team members during the research project, which serves as preparation and testing for ultimately releasing a snapshot of the data and its documentation for future users.

Data users can also increase the effectiveness of their practice by focusing on the planning phase. In particular, they should explicitly identify and seek context needed to support their assessment of the relevance of the data source for their research objectives, the data source’s quality and potential flaws, and how they can appropriately steward and analyze the data to protect the integrity of the data source and its producer. Extra attention to terms of use is needed for data that require protection due to confidentiality, proprietary or national security concerns. In addition, users can promote success for themselves and producers by citing the data source and its producers in scholarly outputs. 

These results emphasize the need to cultivate positive interdependence between data producers and data users, a relationship where the behaviors of each party foster the success of the other party. As a guide, we developed a model that summarizes connection points between producers and users in the data sharing and reuse cycle that are key to enhancing each party’s success. The strategies cited above for reducing burden and increasing effectiveness are meant to foster this success and minimize the likelihood of individualistic actions that promote negative interdependence. For example, if a producer develops the type of documentation needed by future users to properly use shared data and provide credit to the producer, then their downstream impact is improved as other researchers extend their findings and increase the producer’s visibility through citations. The producer can reap strong benefits from their efforts to provide quality documentation and digital objects by implementing methods to capture documentation and check data during the research process (e.g., creating standards, protocols and algorithms to share and update this information internally with their research group before posting it publicly). This reduces total effort in generating data and documentation and increases the quality of shared research outputs. Similarly, users can uphold their end of the relationship not only by citing the data and giving credit to the producers, but also by taking the time to fully understand appropriate uses of the data source and proactively identifying resources to meet computational and security requirements associated with the data.

abstractText:
Women remain dramatically underrepresented in the engineering profession, and far fewer women than men persist in the field. There is considerable evidence that a lack of identification with engineering causes students to drop out despite demonstrated technical skills. Recognition is vitally important to the development of identity and the persistence of women students. Previous research has shown when women engineering students were not recognized by their peers and instructors, they had weaker identities as engineers and did not feel as if they belonged in the culture of engineering. This research will focus on addressing the critical need for improved feeling of recognition for women engineering students. This work will provide insight into strategies that would improve recruitment and retention of women engineering students. The results of this study will be used by engineering educators across the country to help create a positive classroom and campus environment for students, thus increasing the potential retention of underrepresented groups in engineering.

The project has three main goals. Goal 1: Identify factors impacting women civil engineers’ feelings of recognition as civil engineers. Goal 2: Develop targeted recognition activities as interventions to increase women civil engineering students’ feelings of recognition as civil engineers. Goal 3: Determine the impact of interventions on women civil engineering students’ feelings of recognition as civil engineering students and engineering identity development. A mixed-methods approach will be used to examine women engineering students’ identity development over a duration of two years. The research will investigate the effects of targeted recognition activities (interventions) on the women engineering students’ formation of engineering identity. More specifically, the project will determine whether, and to what extent, recognition interventions strengthen the engineering identity of women students in civil engineering. Formal interventions that enable women to be more readily recognized as engineers and to recognize themselves as engineers are an important aspect of recruitment and retention of underrepresented groups in engineering. This project will also help to develop the expertise of the engineering faculty in conducting engineering education research.

Research results are forthcoming in conference presentations and journal papers.

abstractText:
Tenants face particular challenges in the face of disasters, and those challenges have been amplified in the current pandemic. Signed into law on March 27, 2020, the “Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security” (CARES) Act placed a 120-day moratorium on evictions in federally financed multifamily rental properties as well as fees and penalties related to non-payment of rent in an attempt to at least partially ameliorate a potential national housing crisis. In addition, the Act provided some relief to property owners through forbearance provisions on federally-backed mortgages. The Act, along with a patchwork of similar state statutes, created temporary housing stability for renters and provided local governments with a window of time, a window that has ended in many jurisdictions. A direct federal intervention of this scope into local housing policies was necessary given the expectation that individuals isolate at home to protect community health and safety, but also unprecedented, leaving local governments with little direction regarding how to proceed as the moratorium and forbearance programs began to end. Renters and local housing markets are already feeling the strain, and the long-term impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on rental housing stability remains unknown. This Grant for Rapid Response Research (RAPID) study investigates how the unique characteristics of the US housing system, and in particular landlord decision-making within that system, are contributing to rental housing instability during the COVID-19 pandemic. In typical natural disasters, the impact on housing stems from physical damage which creates an immediate negative shock to the housing supply. The pandemic provides a singular opportunity to examine the housing impacts of a disaster that affects demand rather than supply and to parse out the role of landlord decision-making within that context. This study will collect perishable highly ephemeral data from landlords during a particularly uncertain period: COVID-related threats to public health and safety and the corresponding policy interventions are constantly evolving; the economic recession is deepening; and eviction moratoria and expanded unemployment benefits are coming to an end. The findings will help illuminate how landlord decision-making is shaping rental housing stability during the current pandemic while furthering the scholarly understanding of the role of landlords in disaster-related housing stability and recovery more generally. By evaluating the relationship between landlord characteristics and decisions and housing stability outcomes, the study findings will assist local government officials to evaluate existing disaster policy responses and will provide important insights to inform the development new and innovative rental housing stability strategies in the aftermath of disasters. 

This study uses a mixed-methods approach to investigate the question: What factors are influencing the decision making of residential rental property owners during the COVID-19 pandemic? The research will take place in three mid-sized US cities: Lexington, KY; Minneapolis, MN; and Cleveland, OH. These cites, though similar in size, have varied housing stocks, socioeconomic characteristics, and political orientations. The study focuses on landlords, key players in the housing market and therefore in housing stability and post-disaster housing recovery, rather than tenants, and in doing so addresses a significant gap in the disaster and housing literature. Data collection tasks will include (1) an online survey of landlords and property managers identified through local residential rental registries to identify landlord characteristics and any divergence in their responses based on those characteristics; (2) follow up interviews with select willing landlords and property managers to investigate in greater depth their perceptions of COVID-related challenges and the decisions they are making in response to those challenges; and (3) interviews with local planners, public officials, landlord association representatives, and other policy stakeholders to collect their understanding of rental housing problems in the city and local landlord responses to those problems. The research team anticipates that investigating the decisions that landlords are making during and after the COVID-19 crisis will elucidate how those decisions contribute to rental housing stability during and after natural disasters. Further, the analysis will assist disaster scholars in developing new risk models and community resiliency indicators that will be useful in response to future economic shocks and disasters.

projectOutComesReport:
Tenants face distinct challenges in the face of disasters, challenges that were amplified during the COVID-19 pandemic. This RAPID response study investigated how landlord decision-making during the pandemic affected rental housing instability. The study focused on landlords rather than tenants, and in doing so addressed a significant gap in the disaster and housing literature. Our objective was to identify relationships between landlord characteristics (ie, demographic, portfolio, financing) and rental housing outcomes while furthering the scholarly understanding of the role of landlords in disaster-related housing stability and recovery more generally.

This study collected perishable data from landlords from November 2020 ? May 2021, a time when COVID-related threats to public health and safety and the corresponding policy interventions were constantly evolving. Data collection tasks included: (1) an online survey of landlords identified through local residential rental registries; (2) follow up interviews with select willing landlords; and (3) interviews with local planners and other policy stakeholders regarding local rental housing problems and rental property owner responses to those problems. We conducted our study in three mid-sized US cities with existing rental registries: Minneapolis, Minnesota; Cleveland, Ohio; and Tampa, Florida.

The first finding from this study emerged in response to the research design: Rental registries have an important role to play in disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. The existence of rental registry or rental certificate programs (registries), municipal programs where a city maintains a list of rental property owners for inspections and/or business registry purposes, vary state-by-state and city-by-city. Many cities do not maintain a registry, and for those that do, the purpose of the registry, the information included, the comprehensiveness, and the extent to which the registry is available to the public varies. For example, some cities only require short-term rentals to be certified or that property owners register only if they want to file for eviction. Minneapolis, on the other hand, has a rental registry that is accessible online and includes more that 95% of the city?s rental units (based on American Community Survey estimates). This registry includes owner information as well as inspection grades by rental unit. Most cities in the US, however, do not have registries, and property tax records are notorious for keeping the names of individual owners obscured. This means that cities have no way of communicating with rental property owners when a disaster occurs. Our interviews revealed that even when cities had registries that could have been used to communicate with rental property owners during the pandemic, they rarely were used in that way.

Approximately 1750 residential rental property owners responded to the survey across the three cities. The survey results are available through a data dashboard which was created to share the study findings with the public (https://covidrental.design.iastate.edu/). Preliminary analysis focused on the question of landlord stress, which we defined as any negative impact on a property owner?s residential rental business such as rent arrears, difficulty filling vacancies, or an anticipated decline in rental income. In the city of Minneapolis, almost 50% of the respondents identified some form of stress as a result of the pandemic. Our analysis of the Minneapolis data found consistent associations between reported stress and rents, portfolio size, unit quality, and the race of the property owner. Specifically, the more units a person owned, the lower the average rents, and the lower the quality of the unit (based on inspection scores), the more likely the property owner was to experience stress from the pandemic. Black property owners were more likely to experience stress as well. Of the four variables, unit quality had the strongest association.

We conducted nearly 40 follow up interviews with property owners across the three cities. These interviews provided an opportunity to dive more deeply into the question of stress as well as the particulars of individual portfolios and stress responses. These data revealed that the pandemic-related stress that owners experienced had more dimensions than simple tenant-related stress that arose from an inability to collect rents or file evictions. Owners also identified unit-related stress (eg, pre-existing conditions, upkeep, maintenance), business-related stress (eg, financing requirements, concerns with access to credit, property taxes), regulatory-related stress (eg, eviction moratoria, new local code requirements) and stress resulting from personal circumstances (eg, loss of other sources of income, family commitments, location). Further research will identify meaningful property-owner related variables associated with each of these five areas of stress.

This study investigated the relationship between the characteristics and actions of residential rental property owners and rental housing instability during the COVID-19 pandemic. This research contributes to the field by identifying meaningful relationships between property owner characteristics and portfolios and pandemic-related stress and the multi-dimensional characteristics of that stress. Findings regarding the importance and underuse of municipal rental registries suggests an immediate policy window for improving local disaster preparedness.

abstractText:
This research is concerned with the development of mathematical models and corresponding state-of-the-art computational methods for simulating and predicting the dynamics of complex fluid systems, such as those arising from multiphase flows and plasma. The ability to predict the dynamics of these complex fluid systems is of vital importance in understanding a wide range of phenomena such as particulate flow in the atmosphere, fuel sprays in combustion engines, magnetically-confined fusion reactors, laser-plasma accelerators, space weather, and astrophysical events. The underlying physics of such systems are often well-represented by kinetic models that represent the state of the fluid in terms of probability density functions. The main challenge in accurately simulating these kinetic models is that solutions live in a high-dimensional phase space and contain information over wide-ranging spatial and temporal scales. The goal of this research is to develop reduced models that simultaneously capture the important physics and can be more readily solved on modern computer architectures. As part of this research effort, graduate and undergraduate students will be trained in mathematical modeling and computational mathematics. Students from groups that are underrepresented in applied and computational mathematics will be encouraged to participate in the research efforts.
 
The primary objective of this research is to develop accurate and efficient computational methods for solving kinetic models of both polydisperse multiphase flows and plasma flows via entropy-consistent moment closures. The purpose of moment-closure techniques is to reduce high-dimensional kinetic models to more computationally tractable approximations. However, determining a suitable moment closure is a mathematical challenge; a general approach that combines desirable mathematical features remains elusive. This research will pursue two related approaches: (1) using quasi-exponential representations of the underlying kinetic distribution functions, and (2) using delta functions in conjunction with entropy maximization. Novel moment-inversion algorithms and high-order numerical schemes will be developed. The resulting codes will be implemented on massively parallel computers. These techniques will be applied to problems in polydisperse multiphase flows and plasma flows.
