projectOutComesReport:
This project investigated how small clusters of thunderstorms grow into larger systems that produce much of the rainfall that happens in the central United States during the warm season, and examined ways of better predicting these larger systems.  It also examined ways to better predict severe thunderstorm winds, and the sensitivity of numerical weather model simulations of different types of thunderstorms to the grid spacing used in the models.

It was found that the areas of cooling due to rain evaporation that happen in thunderstorms are more intense in model simulations that use 1 km grid spacing instead of 3 km.  Faster growth of thunderstorm systems in the 1 km runs may be related more to rising air that occurs away from the edge of the cold air.  The intensity of the cold air does not work well as a tool to predict which systems will grow much larger in size or not. It was also found that errors in how a model depicts humidity during the evening, just prior to when the large thunderstorm systems typically form can be used to predict errors in where the model will show the thunderstorm system to take place, at least for events where the larger-scale environment is favorable for thunderstorm formation.

For thunderstorm systems that often produce severe wind, known as bow echoes, it was found that at night, it is not the amount of cool air near the ground that determines how intense the winds will be, but instead how unstable the atmosphere is at higher levels, and the best tools for forecasters are some composite parameters that combine several metrics measuring both how unstable the air is, and how winds change with height.  A similar analysis of daytime bow echo cases showed some of the same parameters worked well for prediction of wind intensity, but also the amount of dry air in the lower atmosphere played a bigger role in getting very intense winds than it did at night.  An analysis of model predictions of these bow echoes showed that when 3 km grid spacing was used, bow echoes were usually only successfully simulated if there was a larger-scale weather feature present like a front, or very strong flow at low-levels aimed toward the system.  In 1 km model simulations, more bow echoes were produced, because the model runs were able to create the strong winds without having large-scale features present. 

Finally, model simulations were performed for the 10 August 2020 derecho that caused 12 billion dollars in damage in the central United States.  These simulations found that a new weather forecasting model known as the FV3 failed to forecast the event well when 3 km grid spacing was used, because too many false storms formed in the model the night before the derecho occurred.  Grid spacings that were not as fine, like 13 km and 25 km, did a better job, which is unusual. Normally grid spacings like 3 km work best to obtain the most accurate forecast of a thunderstorm. However, if code that is normally only needed for larger grid spacings to represent thunderstorms was turned on, the false storms were prevented, and an excellent forecast resulted, showing winds nearly as strong as was observed.  This finding has caused the National Weather Service to begin using the code in its test runs of a version of the model that is scheduled to become the official short range model used in the United States in the next few years.

abstractText:
Future power grids, the nation’s most critical infrastructure, will be extremely difficult to manage due to large-scale integration of renewable energy resources. The strategy proposed in this project is aided by new grid technologies (converter-based assets in wind/solar farms and high-frequency sensing devices) that are developed and deployed to allow new real-time control-theoretic algorithms to be implemented with little overhead---while guaranteeing grid stability and resilience. The literature in this area had addressed various scientific research questions, but mostly adopted simplified models that cannot adequately capture the real-time operation of future grids. This project addresses this science gap by developing a new set of real-time algorithms, leading to a more robust operation of future power grids characterized with high penetration of renewable energy resources. These control algorithms can be implemented by grid operators throughout the nation. The project will also include: a) hosting an outreach workshop on renewable energy systems for a low-income, minority-majority, and female-only high school in San Antonio; b) organizing a technical industry workshop that showcases the created algorithms in the state of Iowa; c) disseminating the created scientific methods within the curricula at the University of Texas at San Antonio and Iowa State University.


This project aims at modernizing grid control methods which has traditionally relied on linear systems theory. In particular, the control-theoretic literature addressed a plethora of grid challenges with a focus on linearized, differential equation models whereby algebraic constraints (i.e., power flows) are eliminated. This is in contrast with the more realistic, complex nonlinear differential algebraic equation (NDAE) models. Linearizing grid models around operating points and eliminating algebraic constraints have proven to be a reliable strategy---a trade-off between complexity and tractability. Yet as grids are increasingly pushed to their limits via intermittent renewables, their physical states risk escaping operating regions due to a poor prediction of wind or solar. In lieu of linear differential equation models, control of NDAEs is highly beneficial for grids that are characterized by highly uncertain renewables. This guarantees grid stability for larger operating conditions. Given the limitations of present power system models and the lack of theoretical foundations for control and dynamic state estimation of grid NDAEs, this project will: 1) create a physically representative NDAE model of a power system with a mix of conventional machines and a variety of converter-based technologies; 2) investigate a general theory of dynamic state estimation and robust feedback control algorithms that consider the uncertain nature of power grids modeled via higher-order NDAEs; 3) obtain computationally tractable routines that can be implemented in control centers of power grids. The created theoretical foundations have applications in wide area control, converter-based control, centralized and decentralized and robust dynamic state estimation. This research is critical to guarantee acceptable performance of modern and future power systems and will lead to advancing the state-of-the-art of grid control studies.

projectOutComesReport:
This NSF project has:

(i)  Developed a positive-sequence model of a power converter with grid-forming controls. The converter can be powered by either solar arrays, wind turbines, or battery energy storage. The model of the grid-forming converter is suitable to study the fault ride-through capability of these new class of converter-based resources. The model was coupled to mathematical representations of conventional synchronous machines as well as transmission lines and loads in the positive-sequence domain which resulted in a set of differential algebraic equations. The grid-forming technology was also tested in the electromagnetic transient domain while studying fault-induced delayed voltage recovery events.

(ii) Engineered an active protection systems to prevent dc-link voltage collapse of grid-forming units that are powered by solar photovoltaic arrays which in turn depend on the variability of solar irradiance. It was showcased that grid-forming photovoltaic power plants can lose synchronism during variations of solar irradiance because it can cause dc-link voltage collapse. The protection interfaces with the classical droop-control law for grid-forming operation by automatically reducing the amount of power transfered by the converter from the dc-link into the ac power grid. It was was engineered a method to estimate solar irradiance using: an abstract PV array model, PV current, and dc-link voltage. These controls loops yielded a feedback control algorithm that makes the grid-forming inverter robust to uncertain solar irradiance disturbances.

(iii) Set forth a method to propagate initial-condition uncertainties through nonlinear dynamics of power systems with GFM resources. The method forwards initial condition uncertainties (modeled as multivariate polynomial vectors) in time via an explicit 5th-order Runge-Kutta integration rule.  Further, it was also engineered a grid-forming power plant model that is steered by differentiable two-axis anti-windup proportional-integral (PI) regulators. The model is suitable to propagate initial-condition uncertainties even when current saturation occurs. This contribution is supplemented with an algorithm to expedite the truncated multiplication of multivariate polynomials by mapping  the coefficients of two multiplicand polynomials of a particular degree into the coefficients of a resulting one of the same degree. Further, it was developed a  method to ascertain stability from the calculated polynomial vectors based on contraction theory. The latter approach is significant for future power system operators because the absence of rotors in grid-forming power plants challenges classical transient stability approaches.

(iv) Trained a PhD student as well as developed and delivered a short course to industry with the support of the Electric Power Research Center at Iowa State University. The objective of the course was to control and EMT simulate primary energy resources for grid-forming generation resources.The considered primary energy resources were solar arrays, wind turbines, and battery energy storage.

Overall, the outcomes of this project are significant to support the U.S. strategies to achieve zero emissions by year 2050 and to address grid-forming technical concerns raised by reliability organizations.

abstractText:
The Gulf of Maine is located in the Northwestern Atlantic Ocean. Its waters serve as home to the economically important Atlantic Cod and shellfish industry.  But recent changes to this environment pose a threat to the ecosystem and the commercial fishing industry.  However, only a few long-term records of the environment exist in this area making it difficult to tell exactly when these changes started and how much is related to human activities.  In this project, a team of researchers from three universities will construct a 250-year history of the regional environment by measuring yearly growth bands in local clams and algae.  Chemical fingerprints in these growth bands will be used to determine the water temperature, salinity, biological productivity and pH conditions. This allow scientists to study how natural changes have affected the environment and compare these to changes caused by greenhouse global warming.  This information will inform policy decisions of the newly-formed Maine Climate Council on how to better manage this area. The proposed work will also support training for early career scientists, broaden participation in science programs, and support undergraduate research opportunities. 

Specifically, the team will use a multi-pronged approach using geochemical proxies in two types of high-resolution marine climate archives (clams and crustose coralline algae) to reconstruct past changes in oceanographic conditions, including near surface seawater temperatures, salinity, and pH in the Gulf of Maine through the last 250 years. Geochemical fingerprints (or proxies) preserved in the annual growth bands of clam shells and skeletons of long-lived marine calcifiers have been used extensively as archives of past ocean conditions. Discrete calcium carbonate layers can be sampled from the growth bands of clams and crustose coralline algae for geochemical analysis, generating proxy archive records. These reconstructions of past environmental conditions fill data gaps prior to instrumental records. Hence, the proposed research will potentially yield several multi-centennial, annually-resolved, absolutely-dated datasets of oceanographic variability in the Northwestern Atlantic, including the Gulf of Maine, prior to the Industrial Revolution, which will be used to evaluate the role of Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, and other climate forcings, on observed changes. By combining new data derived from traditional and novel proxies with existing hydrographic records, the relative contributions of source waters into the Gulf of Maine through time will be characterized to better understand the drivers of variability within the Gulf of Maine. Understanding past oceanographic variability in the Gulf of Maine is therefore critical for predicting the likely extent and magnitude of future change, and for planning to safeguard ecosystems and fisheries. Results will be widely disseminated to science and non-science audiences through publications, conference presentations, mentoring programs, coursework, and outreach activities at area schools, museums, and science centers.

abstractText:
Currently, most of the commodity and specialty chemicals used to manufacture many of the nation’s commercial and industrial products are made with fossil fuel feedstocks of crude oil and natural gas using thermochemical reactors. In the nation’s electricity generation grid, renewable electricity from wind and sun has been quickly adopted; for example, Iowa generates 34% of its electricity from wind power. These renewable electricity generators are also promising for providing energy to decarbonize the chemical industry. Integration of renewable electricity and renewable carbon (biomass) for distributed production of chemicals in electrolytic reactors, can store renewable electrons in chemical bonds of valuable organics, the long-term storable form, thus addressing urgent needs for power resilience. However, most commercial electro-syntheses of organics only utilize one of the two electrodes of an electrolyzer for generation of desired products. This project aims to design an innovative flow electrolyzer for pairing electrocatalytic hydrogenation and oxidation of biorenewable feedstock to simultaneously produce valuable chemicals from both cathode and anode, while suppressing the evolution of less valuable byproducts of hydrogen and oxygen gases. Education activities offered by this project focus on training a large body of students across Iowa and the Midwest with electrochemistry and electrochemical engineering topics. Research outcomes will be incorporated into a newly developed course: Electrochemical Engineering, as well as independent research projects for diverse undergraduate students. The team will also participate in Iowa State University’s existing education and outreach programs to train local high school students each summer. The long-term education goal is to produce a new generation of researchers in the fields of electrochemical systems, facing the global competition in advanced chemical manufacturing. 

This fundamental engineering science research project addresses the design of flow electrolyzers that pair the electrocatalytic hydrogenation and oxidation of biomass-derived feedstock at the cathode and anode, while suppressing the evolution of less valuable hydrogen and oxygen gases. The research tasks are: 1) Understand important mechanisms of electrochemical transformations using model catalysts for 2) accurate synthesis of advanced catalysts, so as to 3) rationally design an efficient electrolysis cell to achieve continuous production of valuable furanic chemicals and monomers at ambient temperature, pressure, aqueous electrolyte with mild pH. The project will take as model biomass feedstock molecules furfural and 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF).
The research will acquire new insights into the mechanisms of the electrocatalytic hydrogenation and oxidation of biorenewable furanic compounds, along with advanced understanding of the role of catalyst composition and structure, electrode potential, and electrolyte pH in these electrochemical transformations. It will also provide needed knowledge for rational design of paired electrolyzers for cogeneration of two valuable chemicals from both anode and cathode and develop new approaches for combining electroanalytic methods and online chemical collection and analysis for better understanding and design of electrolytic systems.

projectOutComesReport:
Currently, most of the commodity and specialty chemicals are derived from fossil fuel feedstocks such as crude oil and natural gas, which are produced through thermochemical processes. However, renewable electricity from wind and solar power has been rapidly adopted in the electricity generation grid. In fact, Iowa generates 57% of its electricity from wind power. These renewable electricity generators have the potential to decarbonize the chemical industry. One promising approach is to integrate renewable electricity and renewable carbon (biomass) for the distributed production of chemicals in electrolytic reactors. However, most commercial electro-syntheses of organics only use one of the two electrodes of an electrolyzer for generating desired products.

 

This project designed innovative flow electrolyzers for pairing electrocatalytic hydrogenation and oxidation of biorenewable furanic compounds to simultaneously produce valuable chemicals from both cathode and anode, while suppressing the evolution of less valuable byproducts of hydrogen and oxygen gases. Our goal was to deeply understand electrochemcial reduction and oxidation aldehydes, as well as acquire design principles for efficient paired electrolyzer design.

 

We investigated the furfural reduction on lead electrodes in acidic conditions and identified the pathways for three products: furfuryl alcohol (FA), 2-methylfuran (MF), and hydrofuroin. Our findings showed that the hydrogenation pathway toward FA and MF is influenced by protons (H2O and H3O+). We also discovered that FA and MF have different formation mechanisms due to the product-selective kinetic isotopic effect of H/D and the surface property-dependent hydrogenation/deuteration pathway. Finally, we revealed that hydrofuroin is produced through the desorption of the intermediate as ketyl radicals followed by its self-coupling in the electrolyte, while FA is generated from further hydrogenation of that intermediate.

 

We discovered that electrochemical oxidation of furfural can generate H2 on Cu and Ag electrodes at low anodic potentials. Combined experimental and DFT studies suggested a reasonable barrier for C-H dissociation on Cu surface, mainly through the diol intermediate, with the potential-dependent competition with the Cannizzaro reaction. We further found the electro-oxidation kinetics and catalyst durability can be enhanced by a porous CuAg catalyst prepared by a galvanic replacement method. We demonstrated membrane-electrode assembly-based flow cells for H2 production from both anode and cathode with a remarkable performance: a combined H2 faradaic efficiency (FE) of ~200% and H2 partial current density 390 mA/cm2 at cell voltages of 0.6 V.

 

We also demonstrated a few innovative electrolyzer designs. For instance, we design a flow cell for pairing HMF oxidation and reduction to produce two monomers, and the cell voltage can be reduced from 7.5V to 2.0V as compared to previous H-type cell. We showed a tandem electrocatalytic-catalytic system, that enabled electrolysis at high current density and simultaneously circulates the electrochemically produced H2 for energy-efficient chemical transformations with enhanced energy harvesting from by-product H2. Finally, we designed an anion exchange membrane (AEM)-free, single cation exchange membrane (CEM)-based flow reactor for the synthesis of pure chemical H2O2,

 

In addition to advancing the paired electrolysis of biorenewable feedstock to valuable chemicals, the project also served as a platform to train 9 graduate and 4 undergraduate students. All the doctoral students who were involved in this project and graduated have found employment in engineering. The project has generated 7 articles and delivered 13 presentations. The team worked with ISU’s electric power research center aiming to integrate renewable electricity for distributed chemical manufacturing, and they reached out to local biofuel / biochemical companies to enhance their research impacts. The generated knowledge was integrated into an elective course Electrochemical Engineering to educate students at Iowa State University on energy production, storage, and electrochemical manufacturing.

abstractText:
Part I:  Non-technical Summary
Magnetic materials have shaped our modern society because they are crucial for advances in the fields of renewable energy, electric engines, sensors, and data storage. There are two types of magnetic materials - molecular magnets, composed of isolated molecules, and extended solid or itinerant magnets with infinite frameworks of chemical bonds within the crystal structure. Molecular magnets are appealing due to their synthesis at low temperatures and high tunability but suffer from weak magnetic interactions. In turn, extended solid magnets exhibit strong magnetic interactions and large magnetic moments in the ordered state but have limited tunability. The current project is focused on bridging the gap between molecular and extended solid magnets by synthesizing a unique set of hybrid compounds, which combine advantages of both classes of magnetic materials. In the proposed hybrid compounds, tunable molecular fragments will be sandwiched in between one- and two-dimensional fragments of extended solid magnets. Understanding how structure determines properties is the key step for design of emerging materials. Thus, to achieve significant breakthroughs in the magnetic materials development, we are establishing fundamental relationships between structure and nature of interactions of molecular and extended fragments, and magnetic properties of the produced materials.  In the educational component of the project, chemistry graduate and undergraduate students are engaged in chemistry demonstrations at local elementary schools, the Iowa State STEM Program for Women in Science and Engineering, and the Des Moines Science Center to foster interest of K-12 students and adults in chemistry.  This project is supported by the Solid State and Materials Chemistry Program in the Division of Materials Research.

Part II:  Technical Summary
Exploration of chemical factors that affect magnetic interactions in solids is one of the major steps in the development of novel magnetic materials. Current solid state syntheses lack the predictability and rationality of organometallic and coordination chemistry. To achieve high predictability and rationally design magnetic materials, hybrid magnetic materials comprising infinite Fe-chalcogenide fragments separated by interstitial coordination metal complexes are being developed. In this way, strong magnetic interactions and tunability are segregated into two different sublattices of a hybrid material. The project uses coordination chemistry methodology to tune molecular transition metal amine complexes which are incorporated in between or connected to extended infinite Fe-chalcogenide fragments of itinerant magnets. It is anticipated that chirality and spin-crossover properties of coordination complexes will be translated to the itinerant Fe-chalcogenide fragments. An advantage of the target hybrids is that strong magnetic interactions and large magnetic moments present in the Fe-chalcogenide sublattice will either amplify the weak magnetic signatures of spin-crossover transitions or produce chiral magnets. In the educational component of the project, chemistry graduate and undergraduate students are engaged in chemistry demonstrations at local elementary schools, the Iowa State STEM Program for Women in Science and Engineering, and the Des Moines Science Center to foster interest of K-12 students and adults in chemistry.  This project is supported by the Solid State and Materials Chemistry Program in the Division of Materials Research.

projectOutComesReport:
Expanding the library of known inorganic compounds which hold promise for energy applications has long been a key objective in materials chemistry and engineering. These applications encompass materials that can convert waste heat into electricity (thermoelectrics), function as solar absorbers, as well as optoelectronics, superconductors, and memory storage. Chalcogenide materials are particularly valuable for these purposes. Compared to their oxide counterparts, the chalcogenide chemical space is less explored. Furthermore, due to the limited availability of tellurium in the earth’s crust, there is a growing interest in selenium-containing materials to expand the chalcogenide chemical space by developing sustainable synthetic procedures. Unfortunately, exploration of chalcogenide materials is historically hindered by issues associated with their synthesis: a reliance on highly toxic and/or expensive reactants, and energy-intensive high-temperature synthetic techniques. Given that chalcogenides have potential for revolutionizing the energy sector by providing sustainable and cost-effective energy sources, it is crucial to dedicate research efforts to overcome the aforementioned synthetic challenges. As such, part of this proposal dealt with the development of sustainable synthetic method for activating elemental selenium to enable low-temperature synthesis of functional selenides.

Elemental selenium was dissolved using a sustainable solvothermal method by reacting it with ethanolamine, an easily accessible organic solvent. The resulting solution remains stable in air for  few days before solid selenium starts to precipitate. Reheating the solution causes the precipitate to dissolve thus producing no Se waste. Notably, when the activation process was carried out in an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen), no precipitation occurred even after several months, indicating the high stability of the prepared solution. The activated Se solution was extensively studied using various spectroscopic and spectrometric techniques. The facilely-prepared, cheap, and moderately stable Se precursor solution is a highly viable selenium source for synthesizing metal selenides with improved properties. The selenium solution enabled successful synthesis of various binary metal selenides at near-room temperature, including the polycrystalline β-Ag2Se thermoelectric material, large single crystals of superconducting β-FeSe, solar adsorber CdSe nanocrystals with varying particle sizes (3-10 nm), and nanosheets of PtSe2 – an emergent nanocrystalline layered material. Thus, starting from elemental Se, the developed methodology provides a straightforward and sustainable approach for producing reduced selenium species, which were previously difficult to access via solution chemistry and are essential for synthesizing simple and complex functional selenides with improved properties.

To enhance our understanding of the formation of complex functional selenides and facilitate their synthesis under low-temperature solvothermal conditions, a part of this proposal was dedicated to the development and application of an in situ solvothermal reaction environment at the synchrotron facilities, such as 17-BM beamline at the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory (APS ANL). This reaction environment allows for in situ variable-temperature studies of synthesis of complex materials by collecting powder X-ray diffraction patterns as the reaction progresses. This aids in understanding inorganic reaction mechanism by revealing intermediate and metastable crystalline phases that emerge during the reaction and allows to determine the optimal synthetic conditions required to achieve high selectivity and yield of the target phases. A typical half-hour synchrotron experiment saves months of synthetic optimization work in the laboratory and provides mechanistic insights that can help to understand other chalcogenide systems. The developed methodology was adopted by APS ANL and is anticipated to be expanded to other synchrotron facilities. Insights from in situ studies have steered our understanding of these complex systems and led to the synthesis of diverse functional selenide materials.

This project provided exciting yet educational chemistry demonstrations to the public in Iowa. Project participants presented chemistry on Iowa State University Campus, at local elementary schools, and at the Des Moines Science Center (Spooky Science Halloween) with 1000+ visitors annually. In addition, online educational resources, a series of video tutorials, were created targeting a rookie performer audience, showing the demos, explaining chemistry behind it, and safety aspects performer should be aware of to not hurt a performer or audience members.

abstractText:
The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) global pandemic continue to be a major public health crisis in the U.S. Missing from the academic and policy discussion is the pandemic’s impact on smaller communities. Rural places are still highly susceptible to COVID-19 even in the absence of confirmed cases, as the pandemic may just be taking hold. This makes rural places statistically invisible, creating a false sense of rural immunity. There is an urgent need to understand the health and socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 in understudied rural communities, especially in meat packing towns. Near real-time data collection is needed to understand the full impact of COVID-19 and the effectiveness of recovery efforts, especially among vulnerable rural populations, e.g. older, poor, disabled, immigrant, or minority residents. This project will survey residents of midwestern small towns to: (1) document the health, socioeconomic, and emotional impacts of the pandemic; (2) identify local needs and effectiveness of local and state responses; and (3) understand how impacts, responses, and needs vary across diverse small towns. Findings from the project will inform governmental policies and programs at several levels, thus advancing the health and well-being of rural people and places. 

Rural places are highly susceptible to COVID-19 even in the absence of confirmed cases, making rural places statistically invisible and creating a false sense of rural immunity. And yet social research to date has disproportionately focused upon the urban impact.  This project will survey n=11,716 residents across 65 small towns (between 800 and 10,000 people) using an existing longitudinal rural panel from the Iowa Small Towns Project (ISTP). These ISTP communities are uniquely vulnerable to COVID-19 because they are home to large meat packing facilities, potentially exacerbating preexisting racial marginalization and stigma. The principal investigators will establish an advisory panel comprised of diverse stakeholders who will guide the project. A comprehensive survey and community engagement strategy will be used to effectively oversample meat packing workers and minority residents. Health impacts will include individual COVID-19 physical health issues, access to and use of healthcare, perceived prevalence in the community, and impact on local healthcare systems. Emotional impacts will include standard depression and anxiety scales (CESD-10 and GAD-7), access to and use of mental health services, and general concern about the pandemic’s impact on family and community. Economic impacts will include household employment and income loss, change in spending patterns, access to and use of economic security programs, and local economic impacts. Social impacts will measure how social capital, social support, and quality of life have been affected by the pandemic. Access and trust of COVID-19 information sources will be measured, as will adherence to social distancing. Residents will be asked to rate pandemic preparedness and responsiveness of governments, healthcare providers, local businesses, and community organizations. Findings from the project will inform sociological theories related to social capital, social stress, and socio-economic inequality, particularly related to health and minority status.  All findings will contribute to larger bodies of literature related to rural sociology, which seeks to understand the social dynamics of rural life in the United States.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of our project is to understand the impacts of COVID-19 on rural communities, patterns of resiliency or vulnerability, and responses of people and places to the pandemic. We give special attention to the challenges facing ethnically diverse meat packing towns. We sent multi-language questionnaires to 13,280 housing units across 73 small towns in Iowa in January 2021. A total of 5,229 questionnaires were returned, for an overall response rate (RR2) of 39.4%, with 42.9% for the general sample and 31.0% for persons of color sample.  

Regarding COVID health impacts, we found that nearly 60% were tested for COVID and 25-33% tested positive, with highest positivity among persons of color (POC) and lowest among seniors. Hospitalization rates from COVID were low, mostly 1.5% for whites, 3.0% (2x higher than non-senior whites) for white seniors and whites in poor health, and 7.9% (5x) for POC. Vaccination intentions differed, being highest at 62% for seniors and 47-48% for POC and those poor health, but low at 39% for whites under 65.

COVID mental health impacts differed according to risk. Depression (CESD-10 scale) was far higher than pre-pandemic levels of 6.7%. Those in poor health showed the most signs of depression at 66%, as were POC at 44%. Whites and seniors scored lower, but depression signs were still high at 38%. Anxiety (GAD-7 scale) was also far higher than the 3.1% pre-pandemic level. The most anxious are those in poor health (38%) and POC (30%), but the white rate was half that at 15%, while seniors had the lowest anxiety at 10%.  Many POC have sought mental health services at rates much higher than whites.

Rural people of color suffered major financial and economic impacts from COVID. Rural POC had severe reductions in employment: 48% had hours cut (1.5x higher than non-senior whites), 28% had benefits reduced (3.5x), 26% had pay cuts (1.9x), and 20% were laid off (1.7x).  As a result, rural POC were unable to pay bills: 38% were unable to pay non-housing bills (4.2x), 27% were unable to pay rent (6.8x), and 30% had to use savings to make ends meet (2x). Rural POC also had fallen into debt: 29% took on debt to pay bills (2.2x) and 17% took on medical debt caused by COVID (4.3x).

Overall, the results of the project can be summarized as follows. For rural seniors (whites), COVID-19 had a minimal impact. Many seniors had prior physical and mental health issues, so there was little change during COVID. Seniors likely self-isolated and got the COVID vaccine early, resulted in low COVID  complications. Seniors had few financial concerns because of sizable non-labor retirement income. For rural whites (<65), COVID was experienced as a mental health issue. Depression became a major issue because of reduced socialization among friends, family, and neighbors. Whites were less likely to work in high-risk jobs, were in good physical health, and were generally financially secure. Lack of health and financial impacts were the likely cause of low vaccination rates and skepticism of COVID as a legitimate disease and threat to public health. For the health compromised (whites <65), COVID was a real threat to their physical and mental health. This was the only group whose health significantly worsened during COVID. Isolation and vaccines were not sufficient to prevent COVID complications. Prior vulnerabilities resulted in very high depression and anxiety rates. This group experienced some financial troubles, but non-labor disability income blunted these impacts. Despite limited savings and few means to earn money, most all were covered by insurance, especially Medicaid, reducing medical debt. By contrast, for rural people of color, COVID was a true pandemic that devastated lives and livelihoods. Many POC were connected to the meat packing industry, through work or living in households with workers), placing them at high physical and financial risk. Persons of color were at-risk for COVID due to working conditions and household living arrangements. POC were also more vulnerable because many had limited income and savings, poor English language skills, poorer educations, uncertain legal or work status in the U.S., and many were socially isolated from health and social services provided by the community. POC suffered very high rates of COVID hospitalizations and high medical debt. Many POC were unable to pay rent and had worsening housing situations that put then at risk of being housing insecure. Unlike other rural people, POC experienced job losses and/or major cuts to working hours, wages, and benefits. All of this likely accounted for very high anxiety levels among POC, and many sought mental health services in greater numbers than whites, seniors, or even though in poor health.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is to understand the benefits of inexpensive and high-quality soil fertility and yield maps. Soil testing helps farmers to determine the amount of fertilizer needed for plants. In 2017, total agricultural land in Iowa was 30.5 million acres, and the average farm size was 351 acres. If all farm managers took samples based on the commonly used sampling design, they would spend over $291 million. With the new sampling design, farmers in Iowa may save close to $129 million (44%). During participation in the ISU I-Corps Site program, a key customer discovery finding was that farmers need these more accurate and less expensive maps compared to existing ones in order to fertilize their crops effectively, but without waste. 

This I-Corps project will help to determine if farmers are interested in an alternative sampling design, which can provide low cost analysis of field variations. The technology will have the ability to supply precise management zones from accurate soil maps. The technology will create soil maps with relatively fine resolution (9 sq. meters) compared to the existing maps (2.5 acres). Preliminary results show that kriging can produce a soil map with 9 sq. meters; however, the accuracy of kriging maps (R2 = 0.1) with small sample sizes is remarkably smaller than the proposed maps (R2 = 0.53-0.61). Thus, the nutrient recommendations will remain effective while the costs decrease compared to the current methods (block and kriging).

projectOutComesReport:
Our technology aims to deliver a scalable digital soil map solution that meets the demands of modern commercial agriculture. Agronomists and growers (our end-users) use various tools to balance economic return/profitability and environmental externalities. Our engagement with the National I-Corps revealed that end-users actively seek to use higher quality maps to base their annual decision-making on; however, the tools available to them do not simultaneously deliver on accuracy and resolution. Our findings show that our innovation can decrease the risk of overapplying and underapplying fertilizer for growers by producing high-quality soil fertility maps. Doing so helps growers to apply the right amount of fertilizer in the right place.

High-quality soil information is a fundamental driver of better crop management, which has the potential to lower food costs and improve environmental sustainability. There are many good reasons for growers to invest in soil fertility mapping: nutrient management planning, land use planning, planting decisions, etc. SoilSerdem’s technology will utilize robust machine-learning tools with remotely sensed data to significantly increase the quality of soil data presented to the end-users in terms of accuracy and resolution. To meet the projected global food demand by 2050, production must be increased by 60-70%. This innovation will be a cornerstone to efficient farming of the future.

During the I-Corps customer discovery process (105 interviews), we mapped the relationship between the end-users (growers), influencers (university extension and agronomic consultants), and vendors (retailers) in the commercial agriculture space. Growers working over 100 acres request soil maps from agronomists to inform their nutrient management planning. The main reason that growers prefer to work with agronomists is that they trust agronomists - as an independent information broker - for nutrient management recommendations more than retailers. The best way to reach out to potential customers is by attending trade shows (e.g., Farm Progress Show and Husker Harvest Days) and extension conferences. The team established a cursory network across the USA during this program.

abstractText:
Aircraft icing is one of the most serious weather hazards to aircraft operation in cold weathers. Ice accretion over airframe surfaces can make the aircraft to roll or pitch uncontrollably, and even cause crashes. While a number of systems have been developed for aircraft icing mitigation, current anti-/de-icing strategies suffer from various drawbacks, including being too complex, too heavy or draw too much power to be effective. One promising method to resolve these issues is to utilize plasma actuation for aircraft anti-/de-icing operation. The principal aim of this project is to investigate the underlying physics of plasma discharges interacting with different substances (i.e., air, water and ice) associated with ice accretion process for the development of a new class of strategies for aircraft icing mitigation. The project will also encompass significant educational activities, including a multi-year graduate/undergraduate research program, development of new teaching modules, and an outreach program for local K-12 students, especially those from groups underrepresented in STEM fields, to inspire them to participate in science and engineering studies.

The goal of this proposed research is to conduct a fundamental study to characterize the effects of Dielectric-Barrier-Discharge (DBD) plasma actuation on the coupled unsteady heat and mass transfer during the dynamic ice accretion process. The research tasks include: 1) conduct a fundamental study to characterize the thermodynamic characteristics of DBD plasma actuations under frozen-cold ambient temperatures pertinent to aircraft icing phenomena; 2) examine dynamic interactions between DBD plasma discharges with liquid water and solid ice to gain further insights into the fundamental mechanisms; 3) characterize the effects of the DBD plasma actuation on the coupled unsteady heat and mass transfer over ice accreting airfoil/wing surfaces; 4) explore/optimize design paradigms for the development of innovative, effective, DBD-plasma-based anti-/de-icing strategies for aircraft icing mitigation. In comparison with conventional anti-/de-icing methods, DBD-plasma-based anti-/de-icing approach could have significant advantages, including i) more efficient heating mechanism; ii) faster response time; and iii) lower operation power consumption for anti-/de-icing operation. The research would significantly improve our understanding about the important micro-physical thermal/mass transport processes, which could lead to the development of a new class of DBD-plasma-based, anti-/de-icing strategies to ensure safer and more efficient aircraft operation in cold weathers.

abstractText:
This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the Iowa State University will establish sustainable learning communities of Graduates for Advancing Professional Skills (GAPS) and design a new framework of training that adapts the project management skills from industry to academic research. The program will address two fundamental education research questions: How can project management skill training be integrated with thesis research in graduate education? What is the role (or value) of learning communities in enhancing the training and retention of professional skills and effectiveness of thesis research? Studies suggest that current graduate education focuses too narrowly on thesis research, and graduate students are not well prepared with skills for future work in industry or the academy. However, limited resources and lack of faculty support prevent students from committing to skill training. To address these challenges, this e program will develop innovative training approaches to help students learn and practice project management skills. 

Utilizing the framework of communities of practice, the project will have two major innovations. The first is engaging students with self-directed, learning activities to produce and evaluate new course content as they learn from the curated online modules. The second is practicing the professional skills integrated with the thesis research. This new learning model has the potential to fundamentally change the culture of graduate education, efficiently utilize the current resources, and obtain faculty buy-in. Associated research design will explore factors that may lead to the success of a learning community, help reconceptualize current graduate education and encourage broader adoption of these new approaches within and beyond STEM fields. The evaluation approach is informed by the pragmatic evaluation paradigm, and a variety of data will be collected in the study including program participation data, document analysis, student surveys, and faculty and industry partner interviews. The program will rigorously test over multiple cohort iterations and with control groups the benefits of this approach, including the synergy created between thesis research and professional skill training through the GAPS program. The goal is to disrupt the status quo of graduate education (courses followed by individual research) and build sustainable GAPS communities that can effectively improve professional skills for graduate students. Ultimately, the program will improve graduate student job readiness and placement upon graduation. 

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

projectOutComesReport:
Graduate programs often focus heavily on research, leaving students with limited opportunities to practice essential professional skills such as project management, teamwork, communication, and career planning. The Graduates for Advancing Professional Skills (GAPS) program was designed to enhance the professional and career preparation of graduate students in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). The program filled this need by offering a structured course, workshops, and community-building activities that complemented students’ research training and prepared them for future careers.

GAPS enrolled more than 120 graduate students representing a wide range of STEM disciplines. The program featured a one-credit graduate course where students learned to apply practical project management tools such as project charters, Gantt charts, Critical Path Method, and Work Breakdown Structures directly to their thesis research. In addition, students engaged in activities such as resume-building, mock interviews, and roundtable discussions with alumni and industry professionals. These active learning strategies encouraged reflection, collaboration, and the development of transferable skills.

Evaluation results demonstrated clear benefits. Surveys and focus groups consistently showed that students improved their ability to organize research, manage time, and communicate effectively with advisors and peers. Over 80 percent of participants agreed that GAPS significantly enhanced their professional skills, and more than 90 percent rated the program as highly valuable to their graduate experience. Faculty advisors confirmed that students showed clearer research direction and improved planning. Alumni surveys reinforced the long-term value of GAPS, with graduates reporting that they continued to apply these skills successfully in academic, industry, and government careers.

Beyond the classroom, GAPS built a supportive learning community. Students participated in more than 20 structured social hours, where they practiced leadership and teamwork in informal settings. Workshops and alumni panels provided networking opportunities and helped participants envision diverse career pathways. These activities strengthened students’ sense of belonging and promoted inclusion by encouraging open discussion across different backgrounds and disciplines.

The intellectual merit of the program lies in demonstrating that professional skills training can be systematically integrated into graduate STEM education. Through presentations at national conferences such as the American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) and the American Educational Research Association (AERA), the GAPS team contributed new insights into the effectiveness of active and inductive learning approaches. Findings showed that embedding project management and communication skills into graduate education improves research efficiency, enhances collaboration, and prepares students for leadership roles.

The broader impacts of GAPS extend across the STEM workforce and society. By preparing graduates to lead projects, work effectively in teams, and plan their careers with confidence, the program helps create a workforce that is adaptable and ready to tackle challenges in diverse environments. The emphasis on communication, inclusion, and leadership equips students to contribute positively not only to scientific and technological fields but also to business, healthcare, education, and public service. In this way, GAPS promotes a more prepared workforce that carries forward the principles of collaboration and inclusion into their professional lives.

In summary, the GAPS program demonstrated that professional skill development can be successfully embedded in graduate education and sustained over multiple years. It has left a lasting impact on students, faculty, and the broader STEM community by equipping future scientists and engineers with the tools they need to succeed in research, industry, and beyond.

abstractText:
Many small, deep lakes formed during the melting of continental ice sheets that covered much of the northern hemisphere before 10,000 years ago. It is hard for oxygen to mix into small, deep lakes, which makes them “microbial worlds”, as most aquatic animals can’t live without oxygen. This project will test whether such small lakes that lack oxygen also contain abundant iron, and whether that iron is supplied from the surrounding glacial deposits. With no oxygen, and abundant iron, lake microbes can produce methane out of sinking algal or plant material. Road salt applications near lakes might also cause lakes that did mix to stop mixing, making conditions better for methane-producing microbes. This work will give a better idea how lake shape, microbes, and water chemistry contribute to lake emissions of methane, which is an important but not well-understood contributor to natural greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere. The chemistry of these lakes is also similar to the oceans before 500 million years ago, before animals appeared, and so we can use them to help understand if oceans were producing methane in the past. Undergraduate and graduate students will collect field data from lakes in a rural and urban area in Minnesota (MN) as part of class and research expeditions. The field methods, findings, and data will be shared through traditional (publications and conferences) and non-traditional (YouTube videos, Wikipedia pages) outlets. Workshops in Minneapolis, MN will engage diverse youth, including residents of a historically African American neighborhood adjacent to an urban study lake. Workshops in Itasca State Park, MN, the site of the rural lakes, will engage the visiting public and residents of surrounding counties and nearby Native American population centers.

There are only 22 ferruginous meromictic lakes worldwide identified in the literature, but do more exist? Most of the recognized ferruginous meromictic lakes are postglacial, with groundwater or peatlands a hypothesized, but unverified source of iron. More than a dozen postglacial lakes in two field areas in Minnesota (MN) will be evaluated for meromixis and ferruginous conditions, giving insight into how land use changes enhance meromixis. Detailed iron budgets will be constructed for two lakes to identify and quantify iron sources. Many ferruginous meromictic lakes have a subsurface chlorophyll a maximum layer at the iron-oxygen redoxcline, and the contribution of this layer to primary productivity and oxygen production will be quantified in two lakes. Furthermore, rates of methanogenesis, methane fluxes, and the contribution of methane to the organic carbon degradation will be quantified in two lakes to better constrain carbon fluxes under ferruginous conditions. The results of these activities will better delineate 1) the extent of meromictic ferruginous lakes, 2) fluxes of water and elements between surface and groundwater reservoirs, 3) and carbon cycling under ferruginous conditions, which predominated in Earth's past oceans and influenced the oxidation of Earth's surface.

abstractText:
PART 1:   NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Proteins are extremely important biomolecules involved in practically every biological process. Although synthetic materials that bind peptides and proteins in aqueous environments are highly desirable, they are difficult to produce due to complexity of biological peptides. The research group of Professor Yan Zhao at Iowa State University develops novel antibody-mimicking polymeric nanoparticles for sequence-specific recognition of peptides. These materials are expected to enable numerous applications in chemistry and biology including identification of functional residues responsible for Alzheimer’s disease, regulation of enzymatic catalysis, and purification of peptides and proteins. The research trains student researchers into professional scientists by exposing them to a wide range of skills in biomaterials science, physical organic chemistry, supramolecular chemistry, and polymer chemistry.


PART 2:   TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Proteins are extremely important biomolecules involved in practically every biological process. Although synthetic materials that bind peptides and proteins in competitive aqueous environments have numerous applications in chemistry and biology, they are difficult to produce because of complexity of the guest, subtle structural differences among some amino acids, and difficulty in molecular recognition in water. This project, funded by the Biomaterials Program of the Division of Materials Research, supports Professor Yan Zhao of Iowa State University to develop antibody-mimicking polymeric nanoparticles for sequence-specific recognition of peptides. The materials are prepared through molecular imprinting within cross-linked surfactant micelles and can be tuned systematically in their molecular recognition. With abilities to distinguish closely related amino acid residues, they can be used to probe functional roles of specific sequences in a long peptide, as well as flexible loops catalytically relevant in an enzyme. By their strong and tunable binding for peptides, they enable facile purification of peptides and proteins from complex mixtures.

projectOutComesReport:
Proteins are extremely important biomolecules involved in practically every biological process. Although synthetic materials that bind peptides and proteins in competitive aqueous environments have numerous applications in chemistry and biology, they are difficult to produce because of complexity of the guest, subtle structural differences among some amino acids, and difficulty in molecular recognition in water.

The PI’s group had developed a novel class of polymeric nanoparticles that resemble proteins in their size, hydrophilic exterior, and hydrophobic interior. They contain tailor-made pockets that can bind a range of biologically interesting molecules including peptides and proteins. They are synthesized and purified in <2 days, without any special techniques. They frequently display tens of nanomolar binding affinities in water for biological peptides with over a dozen amino acids. Closely related residues including leucine/isoleucine, arginine/lysine, phenylalanines/tyrosine could be distinguished. In this project, the PI’s group used different strategies to enhance the binding affinity of these nanoparticles, making them useful antibody-mimics for protein purification and isolation. They also demonstrated their usage as “sequence scanners” to probe functional roles of specific sequences in a long peptide or full protein. Their strong binding affinities for peptides allow them to be used as “protecting agents” in protease digestion, allowing selective hydrolysis of a particular residue (e.g., K or R) in a peptide with multiple such residues. Similarly, they allow precise control of posttranslational modifications of peptides and proteins.

These antibody-mimicking nanoparticles tolerate high temperature, organic solvents, extreme pH, and long-term storage. They have the potential to replace expensive, fragile antibodies in many applications. As a result, the research provides an extremely useful set of tools for handling peptides and proteins, and is expected to impact both fundamental research and technological applications.

The research helps train students as future scientists. The multidisciplinary research requires the students to acquire a broad range of skills including supramolecular chemistry, organic synthesis, biology, physical organic chemistry, and polymer chemistry.

The PI includes the biomimetic research in his graduate and undergraduate classes. He also uses his previous industrial experience to help students in his class to better prepare for industrial career. In the undergraduate organic class, he illustrates how “smart” synthetic materials can be designed for molecular recognition (in sensory applications), temperature detection, and catalysis (in enzymatic mimicry). He helps non-science students understand how chemists learn from nature and develop useful materials for technological and biomedical applications. The PI has participated in multiple outreach activities on campus and through partnership with external organizations.

abstractText:
Most insects carry bacteria that live within their cells; these bacteria are inherited from their mothers. The bacteria may manipulate their insect hosts’ reproduction in ways that improves the health or number of female hosts carrying the bacterium. Relevant to this study, these bacterial “symbionts” can sabotage host sperm such that fertilized eggs laid by females without the bacterium die early in life (“cytoplasmic incompatibility,” or “CI”). Currently, two common, unrelated bacteria are known to cause CI in insects: Wolbachia, and Cardinium hertigii, the focus of this study. The main goal of this project is to discover the molecular mechanism by which Cardinium causes CI in insects. The benefits of this work are at least two-fold. Bacteria such as Cardinium target animal cell division, a fundamental process that can be understood better when examining how Cardinium interferes with it. Secondly, CI-causing bacteria may be used for pest or vector management. The CI agent Wolbachia reduces the susceptibility to viruses of insects that carry it, and is currently being introduced around the world to mosquito populations, with major implications for reduction of vector-borne disease and the global bioeconomy. The project will also provide engaging science education targeted for under-represented groups through outreach programs for elementary school (U Arizona Insect Discovery and Insect Festival), high school (production of a book “Animal Manipulating Parasites at NC State, and Iowa State George Washington Carver Internship program) and undergraduate students (via research opportunities at all three institutions). 

For Cardinium strains that infect Encarsia spp., parasitic wasps of whiteflies, genomic and transcriptomic studies have identified candidate genes that are likely to be important in CI and/or symbiosis. The central hypotheses are that (1) Cardinium effector proteins involved in modifying host DNA during spermatogenesis are associated with the testes, and other Cardinium effectors involved with rescue of modified sperm are present in the ovaries of infected wasps, (2) the role of these proteins can be inferred by identifying the host proteins they interact with and (3) that the B vitamin biotin has a critical role in CI and/or the symbiosis. The project presents a unique opportunity to test these hypotheses with a diverse array of approaches, in four objectives: (1) Compare Cardinium localization and CI candidate gene expression in male pupal Encarsia, the “modification” stage, with patterns observed in adults.(2) Identify Cardinium and Encarsia proteins involved in CI with differential proteomics. (3) Use heterologous expression to identify interacting host proteins of CI candidate proteins. (4) Investigate the role of Cardinium synthesized biotin in modification of host proteins. This project will shed light on the sophisticated CI reproductive manipulation by Cardinium. Cardinium has received comparatively little attention, but produces a virtually identical CI phenotype to Wolbachia with what appears to be completely independent eukaryote-interacting genes, a plasmid and not a phage, and an unusual type 6 secretion system. What is learned about Cardinium candidate gene function, expression and host targets will illuminate CI and symbiosis in both systems.

projectOutComesReport:
Many insects carry bacteria that are inherited from their mothers. These symbiotic bacteria live within the insects’ cells. Several symbiotic bacteria manipulate their insect hosts’ reproduction in ways that favors their transmission to the next generation. Some of these symbionts sabotage host sperm such that fertilized eggs laid by females without the bacterium die early in life (“cytoplasmic incompatibility,” or “CI”). In this interaction, eggs that contain the bacterium are able to “rescue” the sperm and normal development occurs. Of the six bacteria known to cause CI, Wolbachia is best studied, and genes involved in causing CI in Wolbachia have been discovered. Cardinium hertigii, the focus of this project, causes CI without the same genes Wolbachia uses. The overall goal of this proposal was to discover the genes involved in CI in Cardinium.

We analyzed the localization of two different CI-causing Cardinium strains in the reproductive tract of pupae and adult Encarsia wasps and found that the two different Cardinium strains show distinct patterns in where they are found in the reproductive tract. Further, the finding that sperm development is complete by the end of the pupal stage indicated that pupal males should be examined for Cardinium protein expression.

We developed a protein sequence database for both the symbiont and the host, critical for protein identification. This database will also be highly valuable beyond this project as a reference for other scientists working with Encarsia wasps.

We detected Cardinium proteins in whole pupal and adult Encarsia wasps and in Encarsia tissues such as ovaries and testes. Among the proteins detected, five were most abundant and showed expression patterns that were indicative of being potentially involved in CI.

These five proteins were cloned and expressed in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) to investigate if these proteins have a toxic effect on yeast cells. We reasoned that a protein secreted by Cardinium into sperm may serve as a toxin during early cell division of the embryo if no Cardinium are present in the egg to neutralize the toxin. Since cell division in yeast is similar to cell division in animals we used yeast cells to test if expression of suspected Cardinium toxin proteins would lead to toxicity in yeast. Out of those five proteins, one (CAHE_0406) resulted in a toxic effect when expressed in yeast cells. Homologs of this protein in other Cardinium strains that were similar (but not identical), did not show a toxic effect to yeast cells. A protein encoded by the gene adjacent to CAHE_0406, CAHE_0405, was detected in pupal testes in much lower quantities than CAHE_0406. This gene did not have a toxic effect on yeast and is currently being evaluated as a possible “rescue” or “antidote” gene.

Broader Impacts

As part of the project, Dr. Eleanor Spicer-Rice, together with the project team, developed a book about microbes and animals for middle school age student and the book was picked up by MIT Kids Press, an imprint of the well-established children’s publisher Candlewick Press. The book was released in May 2023 and has been very successful. It is titled “Unseen Jungle: The Microbes That Secretly Control Our World”. The book features many engaging stories on the important and weird things that microbes do particularly in interaction with animals and plants. Additionally, the book features five interviews with scientists from diverse backgrounds including an interview with the PI Martha (Molly) Hunter.

The project also supported several other training and outreach activities. The PhD student employed in the Hunter laboratory as a graduate student and first year postdoc went on to complete a postdoc and is now transitioning to a tenure track faculty position. Two graduate students have been supported in the Schmitz-Esser and Kleiner laboratory and have completed or are completing first authored manuscripts. Five undergraduates were employed on the project in the Hunter laboratory, two in the Schmitz-Esser laboratory and two in the Kleiner laboratory. The Schmitz-Esser lab hosted two Hispanic high school students through the Iowa State University Science Bound Internship program for underrepresented groups for a six-week summer internship. Hunter and the graduate student in the Hunter laboratory both participated for multiple years in the Arizona Insect Festival, a one-day outreach event to the local community which attracts between three and five thousand people, mostly families, to engage in exhibits and activities showcasing research on insects and insect diversity. They also both participated in Insect Discovery, a semester long series of interactive workshops about insect diversity and behavior for elementary school children.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of technology, called freeze concentration, to produce potable water from high-salt waters or seawater, and to recover water from or concentrate valuable products in industrial process waters. The impact of this technology includes making production of potable water or water recovery more sustainable, energy-efficient and environmentally friendly. Utilities may recover water from their waste streams and increase the volume of water produced and minimize waste discharge. Reducing water use in food processing industries creates more sustainable operations while reducing the cost of production. The overall commercial impact of the technology is to maximize water recovery, reduce discharge of waste streams and protect and maintain precious raw water resources.   

This I-Corps project is based on the development of freeze concentration (FC) technology where ice is formed and separates from aqueous waste streams with a high degree of salts or valuable products exclusion. Ice formed is recovered, melted and reused or returned for further treatment. Since the latent heat of fusion needed to freeze water is less than the energy needed to evaporate water (thermal) or to pump seawater through a semi-permeable membrane (RO), FC may be an energy-efficient process. Laboratory results showed that about 70% of the brine waste stream (total dissolved solids of 2600 mg/L) from an RO treatment plant water may be recovered as potable water using the FC technology - increasing the overall water yield of the RO treatment plant from 83% to 95%. The overall goal of the research is to optimize the operating conditions of the FC technology to maximize the amount of water produced (i.e., reduce the waste stream), lower the cost or energy needed to produce a unit (liters or gallons) of water, and to explore optimization parameters for technology translation.

projectOutComesReport:
The project objective was to assess the market sectors for the adoption and commercialization of the progressive freeze concentration (PFC) technology. The PFC technology uses water freezing to produce fairly pure ice to separate the salts and water from highly saline aqueous solutions.  Some potential applications of the PFC technology include production of potable water from seawater and brackish water.  Current PFC technologies treats the aqueous solutions in a batch mode followed by physical or mechanical recovery of the ice.  The project involves conducting Interviews with practitioners, engineers and business owners on the feasibility and market applications of the technology.  Outcomes of the interviews indicated that the PFC technology would be most competitive in niche market areas where there are limited technologies available in the disposal of highly concentrated aqueous streams such as desalination reject solutions and in the food processing industry for the concentration of useful products in aqueous solutions. The PFC would be less competitive in the mass production of potable water from seawater or brackish water which currently uses reverse osmosis and thermal desalination processes.  Development of a continuous flow system plus a fundamental understanding of the operating conditions that promote maximum ice formation with minimal salts entrapment will further enhance the competitiveness of the PFC technology.

abstractText:
The objective of this project is to create a physics-based probabilistic prognostics platform for lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries. Li-ion battery technology is playing an increasingly important role in realizing wide-scale adoption of hybrid and electric vehicles, and renewable energy sources. Successful development of the proposed platform will produce major advancements in extending battery life while ensuring battery safety. Advances in energy storage management could reduce the costs and promote the wide-scale adoption of hybrid and electric vehicles and renewable energy sources, which in turn will reduce the dependence of our nation on foreign sources of energy. The research findings will be disseminated to the battery industry, main stakeholders, and decision makers through collaboration with an industry leader in battery safety. An inclusive education and outreach plan will help (1) train a globally competitive workforce in battery reliability modeling by incorporating research findings into classroom teaching, (2) provide research experiences to undergraduate and K-12 students with an emphasis on increasing the participation of women and underrepresented minorities, and (3) raise public awareness about battery reliability and safety by giving talks to the local communities. 

The novelty of the proposed prognostics platform is its ability to integrate mechanistic degradation analysis into remaining useful life prediction using probabilistic models. More specifically, model-based smoothing and learning are adopted, in conjunction with bias-corrected half-cell models, to infer the degrees of degradation from noisy voltage and current measurements. This is followed by physics-based prognostics, where model-based tracking is used to predict future degradation trajectories and remaining useful life. The resulting prognostics approach leverages a combination of physical knowledge and sensor data to achieve gains in prediction accuracy and robustness. The proposed platform will advance the field of battery health management by furthering understanding on: (1) how to validate mechanistic half-cell models using relatively few expensive experiments; (2) how to predict the long-term degradation using only early-life data; (3) the role of physics in designing prognostics approaches; and (4) the coupling effects of degradation modes on capacity fade and failure.

projectOutComesReport:
This project developed and validated a physics-based probabilistic prognostics platform to enable proactive health management of lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries. Health diagnostics and prognostics are essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of Li-ion batteries across diverse applications, such as medical devices, electric vehicles, and stationary energy storage systems. Methods and algorithms in the platform can be integrated into battery management systems to estimate the state of health, quantify degradation modes, forecast degradation progression, and predict remaining useful life. Research activities at Iowa State University and the University of Connecticut (UConn) focused on three main thrusts: (1) validating physics-based half-cell models that capture how degradation modes affect a cell’s voltage response, (2) benchmarking model fitting strategies and physics-informed machine learning approaches for non-destructive degradation diagnostics, and (3) developing physics-informed machine learning approaches for capacity forecasting and remaining useful life prediction.

 

This project has produced the following key results.

  • We validated a half-cell model using long-term high-precision cycling data for implantable-grade Li-ion cells of the lithium cobalt oxide (LCO)/graphite chemistry. Additionally, we developed and validated a half-cell model for the lithium iron phosphate (LFP)/graphite chemistry using data from custom-fabricated coin half-cells and full-cells. A unique attempt in our LFP/graphite model validation effort was collecting data from coin full-cells fabricated with known amounts of degradation modes emulated during cell fabrication.
  • We benchmarked multiple half-cell model fitting (model-based) and physics-informed machine learning (data-driven) approaches for diagnosing degradation modes of aged Li-ion cells. These tool provie a robust foundation for automated, non-destructive degradation diagnostics.
  • We designed and validated a physics-informed recurrent neural network capable of forecasting capacity degradation under time-varying loading conditions. This physics-informed machine learning approach captured changes in degradation trends associated with first- to second-life transitions, which conventional machine learning approaches often fail to capture.
  • We extended the application domain of early life prediction to aging scenarios with varying discharge rates and depths of discharge. This extension addressed a known gap in the literature where most pror studies focused on cycling aging under fixed discharge profiles.

 

The broader impacts are the following. (i) The benchmarking of half-cell model fitting and physics-informed machine learning provided insights and best practices crucial to promoting industrial adoption of non-destructive battery degradation diagnostics. (ii) The physics-informed recurrent neural network approach provides an effective and generalizable method for forecasting capacity fade under time-varying loading conditions (e.g., battery repurposing for second-life applications). (iii) The project contributed to open science by releasing two aging datasets: (a) one comprising 64 commercial 18650 LFP/graphite cells aged under time-invariant cycling conditions, and (b) another comprising over 80 cells, to be shared in phased releases beginning in July 2025, aged under cycling conditions simulating first- to second-life transitions. (iv) Six undergraduate and six Ph.D. students contributed to the project and gained hands-on experience in battery testing, data analysis, and machine learning. (v) Research outcomes were integrated into curriculum improvements, including the addition of two chapters on machine learning to a graduate-level course on reliability and prognostics at UConn. (vi) The team shared findings with the broader community through publications, invited conference talks, and seminars at universities and industry organizations.

abstractText:
This project develops science-driven modeling and decision-making algorithms for precision agriculture, with associated cloud-based implementations.  This project would increase the potential for more efficient agricultural systems through the development of more accurate and larger scale models, data collection, and ultimately a software infrastructure that farmers could use for real-time monitoring of their crops.     

The project is derived from scientific questions in sustainable agriculture, sensor networks, decision sciences, data science, and machine learning. The primary innovations are applications of grid-based soil parameters using incomplete data, machine learning-based time series analysis, and optimization problems to estimate the optimal mix of inputs for nutrients and irrigation. These applications are likely to have wide usage among the precision agriculture community.  The cyberinfrastructure, MyGeoHub, is a cloud-based service that users can access through web browsers and leverages an existing infrastructure.

This award by the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure is jointly supported by the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
